paragraphs.text: (1) A court action may be tried by (a) a jury trial under Division 1.1, (b) a judge alone, or (c) a judge alone at a streamlined trial under Division 5. (2) Subject to Division 5, unless the Chief Justice directs that the mode of trial shall be by jury, or in part by jury and in part by judge alone, the trial must be by judge alone. Alta. paragraphs.text: 8.2. Request for jury trial

sentences.text: Request for jury trial

paragraphs.text: (1) An application for a jury trial under section 17 of the Jury Act must be made (a) by written request to the Chief Justice, and (b) before an application is made to the court clerk or a judge to set a trial date. (2) The request for a jury trial must be accompanied with an affidavit that addresses the following issues to the extent that they are applicable: (a) whether expert evidence will be called, and if so, how many experts are expected to be called; (b) the areas of knowledge or experience on which the experts will give evidence; (c) whether interpreters will be required; (d) the number of court days required for the trial if a jury trial is ordered. (3) The Chief Justice may fix a time for the hearing of an application for a jury trial and may make any directions as to the filing of materials as the Chief Justice considers appropriate. (4) If the Chief Justice grants an order directing that a trial be by jury, the order may be with or without conditions and must set the number of days to be initially reserved for the jury trial. (5) Within one month after an order is granted directing that a trial be by jury, the parties must apply to the Chief Justice for appointment of a case management judge.

sentences.text: Deposit for jury

paragraphs.text: (1) When the Chief Justice grants an order directing that a trial be by jury, the party who made the request must, unless otherwise ordered, within 10 days after the date the order was granted, deposit with the court clerk a sum of money that the court clerk considers sufficient to pay the jury's expenses, and if that sum is later determined to be insufficient, on notice from the court clerk, pay any further sum that the court clerk determines in accordance with the Jury Act Regulation (Alta. Reg. 68/83). (2) Any money remaining after the court clerk pays the jury's expenses must be returned to the person who paid it. (3) If the deposit for jury expenses is not paid, the trial must proceed without a jury unless the Chief Justice otherwise orders.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.3:1 Rule 8.3 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.3. Letter of Credit Acceptable The modern rule of interpretation is that words in legislation must be given their ordinary, plain meaning save when to do so would be disharmonious with the object of the statute. The object of the statute here clearly is to secure to the Government of Alberta the cost of panelling a jury. The word “money” therefore should be interpreted to mean money or money's worth. Accordingly, the Queen's Bench and the Clerk have authority to accept a letter of credit or other form of security. On the question of the adequacy of the security, it is noteworthy that this attack was brought not by the Clerk [but] by the party opposite. The risk here is run by the Government of Alberta and not the defendant. We are informed that the Clerk often accepts such letter as security. It is correct, as Mr. Sabey argues, that a letter of credit holds a risk in that it is a mere promise to pay by a financial institution, as opposed to actual currency. This is, however, not an unreasonable risk, particularly when the letter is issued by a Government agency. Sayers v. Shell Canada Resources Ltd. (1984), 64 A.R. 319 at 320 (C.A.).

paragraphs.text: 8.4. Trial date: scheduled by court clerk
paragraphs.heading: Part 8. Trial

sentences.text: Trial date: scheduled by court clerk

paragraphs.text: (1) The parties may, in Form 37, request the court clerk to schedule a date for trial. (2) The request must contain at least the following information unless otherwise directed by the Court: (a) the anticipated number of witnesses, including the number of expert witnesses; (b) the anticipated length of trial; (c) a copy of the pleadings and particulars, if any, for the judge's use at trial; (d) if applicable, the order directing that the trial be by jury; (e) the certifications required by subrule (3); (f) any administrative requirements for the trial; (g) any potential conflict of interest a judge may have and the reasons for it. (3) In addition to the requirements of subrule (2), the parties requesting a trial date must (a) provide (i) a certificate that the parties have participated in at least one of the dispute resolution processes described in rule 4.16(1), or (ii) a copy of an order made under 4.16(2) waiving the dispute resolution process requirement, (b) certify that questioning under Part 5 is complete, (c) certify that any expert reports have been exchanged and the process described in Part 5, Division 2, including questioning of experts, is complete, (d) certify that any medical examination and report under Part 5, Division 3 is complete, (e) certify that any undertaking given by a person questioned under Part 5 has been discharged, (f) certify that they will be ready for trial by a specified date, (g) in the case of a jury trial, certify that the deposit required under rule 8.3 has been paid, (h) certify that all amendments to pleadings have been filed and served, and (i) certify that all applications related to the action have been disposed of and no other pre-trial steps are required. (4) If the court clerk is satisfied that subrules (2) and (3) have been complied with, the court clerk must schedule a trial date. (5) If the parties cannot certify as to the matters referred to in subrule (3) but are satisfied that the matter will be completed or undertaking discharged in a timely way, the parties must so disclose and may request the court clerk to schedule a trial date. (6) If the court clerk is satisfied that the parties will or are likely to be ready by the proposed trial date, the court clerk may schedule a trial date, but if the court clerk is in doubt about any matter, the court clerk must refer the matter to a judge for directions or decision.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.4:1 Rule 8.4 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.4. 1. Costs for Contravention In Tan v. Swyrd, 2013 ABQB 229, 2013 CarswellAlta 522, 560 A.R. 214, 89 Alta. L.R. (5th) 369, Justice Wakeling considered the costs consequences of a plaintiff contravening Rule 8.4(3). His Lordship said, at paragraphs 47–68: 47 Rule 8.4(3)(c) of the new rules states that a party who files a form 37 request must “certify that any expert reports have been exchanged” and that the process described in Part 5, Division 2, including questioning of experts, is complete. Form 37 contains a signature block for counsel. 48 This rule is designed to reduce risk that a party will seek an adjournment of a trial because a necessary expert's report has not been served on another party in a timely manner. A last minute adjournment prejudices not only the parties in the action directly affected by the adjournment but potentially other litigants whose actions are trial ready. A trial date may never be used. Other actions that had back-up status may settle or the counsel or witnesses may not be able to adjust their schedules on short notice. Rule 8.4(3)(c) protects all litigants for whom a trial date is a valuable commodity. The fact that a very small percentage of actions are ever tried does not diminish the harm the court system suffers when a trial date is not used. 49 What does “certify” mean in this context? 50 Plaintiff's counsel argued that a lawyer could file a form 37 request notwithstanding that his client had not served on the other party all the experts' reports the client intended to rely on: “Form 37 states that ‘all expert reports have been exchanged’, the [sic] fair reading of this paragraph would be that it certifies that the parties have exchanged their expert reports in their possession at the time of signing and does not as such preclude the exchange of future expert reports” (emphasis in the original). 51 This argument is unsound. 52 First, it completely disregards the ordinary meaning of “certify”. “Certify”, according to Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged (1971), means “1: to attest esp. authoritatively or formally … (b): to present in formal communication, esp. in a document under hand or seal … (c): to confirm or attest often by a document under hand or seal as being true … (d): to attest officially …”. Combining this definition and the text of rule 8.4(3)(c) results in this conclusion: a party may file a form 37 request only if her counsel has carefully considered whether experts reports are needed and, if they are a necessary part of her client's case, she has served on the other party all the experts' reports on which the client intends to rely at trial. A declaration that is not the product of deliberation is of no value. 53 A lawyer who signs a certificate for her client is not vouching for the veracity of the statements the other party certifies to be true. 54 Second, the argument fails to take subrules 8.4(5) and (b) of the new Alberta Rules of Court into account … Subrules 8.4(5) and (6) explicitly direct counsel who has not exchanged all experts' reports to notify the court clerk of this deficiency. This information allows the court clerk to determine whether the proposed exchange time-lines are reasonable. It is the court clerk's job to review form 37 and decide whether an action will be placed on a trial list. The court clerk and a judge cannot make a rational decision if parties provide inaccurate information. 55 Third, the plaintiff's position fails to recognize that rule 8.4(3)(c) calls upon counsel, in an official court document, to confirm the existence of a fact, critical to the court clerk's assessment of whether an action is trial ready. Rule 8.6 of the new rules, the provision which limits the circumstances under which a trial may be adjourned, reinforces the importance of counsel's certificate. A lawyer is an officer of the court on whose word others in the court system must be able to rely in making important decisions. Legal Professional Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-8, s. 102(2) (a Law Society member is an officer of the Court of Queen's Bench); Rondel v. W., [1966] 3 All E.R. 657, 665 (C.A.) (“[A]n advocate … is a minister of justice equally with the judge”); Hutchinson v. Stephens, 48 E.R. 461, 464 (Ch. 1837) (counsel perform “truly honourable and important services … as ministers of justice, acting in aid of the Judge before whom they practice”); A. Scalia & B. Garner, Making Your Case: The Art of Persuading Judges 33 (2008) (the United States Supreme Court considers a great advocate the tenth justice); Wakeling “The Oral Component of Appellate Work”, 5 Dalhousie L.J. 584, 588 n. 18 (1979) (“As an officer of the court the advocate is obliged to play a role in the law making process”) & Great Australian Gold Mining Co. v. Martin, 7 Ch. D. 1, 10 (C.A. 1877) (a statement counsel signs must be accorded the “greatest possible respect”). The Law Society of Alberta's Code of Conduct declares that this concept is fundamental, recording as its first principle that a “lawyer has a duty to carry forward on the practice of law and discharge all responsibilities to … tribunals … honourably and with integrity”. As one would expect, the Code of Conduct appreciates that “[p]ublic confidence in the administration of justice and in the legal profession may be eroded by a lawyer's irresponsible conduct”. Code of Conduct (2012 version). It is not unusual for court rules to incorporate counsel's certificate into a court procedure. For example, Form M of the Court of Appeal of Alberta's practice directions insists that counsel certify that she has “personally checked the contents of the appeal digest and found them to be complete”. Counsel is in the best position to provide this necessary information. Form 25B of the Rules of the Supreme Court of Canada obliges counsel to certify, in part, “whether there is, pursuant to an order or legislation, a ban on the publication of evidence or the names or identity of a party or witness”. Again, counsel is in the best position to bring this important information to the court's attention. In these two cases, counsel's certificate allows the court system to proceed with a high degree of comfort that foreseeable problems will not occur. D. Plaintiff's Counsel Was Not in a Position To Certify That All Expert Reports Had Been Served. 56 The plaintiff's counsel was not in a position to certify that all expert reports had been served when the plaintiff filed form 37. None of the nine experts' reports which the plaintiff estimated she would introduce at trial had been served on the defendants when plaintiff's counsel signed the form 37 request. 57 The plaintiff's counsel acknowledges in his written argument the existence of the underlying facts which made it impossible to certify that the parties had exchanged all expert reports: The Plaintiff served her Opinion Statements under Rule 5.35 on June 11, 2012. All expert reports generated to this point in time were appended to these expert reports. When Form 37 was filed eight months prior, the Defendant knew that Rule 5.35 production had not yet occurred, and at no point insisted on strict compliance with the new rules which required this exchange to be completed before the Form could be signed and filed. … When it became clear that settlement … was not in the cards, the preparation of the 5.35 statements commenced resulting in the service of the same by June 11, 2012. … …[B]oth counsel signed Form 37, confirming that all experts reports have been exchanged, however both counsel knew at the time that the 5.35 exchange had not occurred. (emphasis added) 58 I commend counsel for his candid concession. 59 I have not considered whether the defendants' counsel was in a position to sign form 37. This is not an issue before me. The defendants are not seeking from the plaintiff reimbursement for any expert fees. But I do note that defendants' counsel asserts in his brief that “[t]he plaintiff had the Defendants' Expert reports, respectively, on January 28, 2011 and August 24, 2011”. My review of the filed material did not confirm that the defendants served rule 5.35 experts' reports on the plaintiff on those days. Perhaps they were not included in the record. I did discover two service letters dated January 28, 2011 and August 24, 2011 which invoked rule 5.44 of the new Alberta Rules of Court. 60 Rule 5.44(3)(a) directs a party causing a medical examination to be conducted to “on request, deliver promptly to each of the other parties a copy of the detailed written report of the health care professional's findings and conclusions”. By complying with rule 5.44(3)(a) a party is not serving on the other side an expert's report referred to in rules 5.34 and 5.35. Rule 5.34 prescribes the format of an expert's report. An expert's report must comply with Form 25 unless the parties agree to a modified format. There is no similar requirement for a rule 5.44(3)(a) written report of a health care professional. Good practice no doubt suggests that a rule 5.44(3)(a) report be referred and attached to a rule 5.34(a) expert's report. 61 I restate a point I made earlier. 62 A counsel who signs a form 37 request certifies that she has carefully considered what role experts will play in the proof of her client's case and that her client has served on the other party all experts' reports on which the client will rely. Her certificate does not reflect her assessment of whether other counsel is in a position to sign a comparable certificate. In some circumstances, professional courtesy may cause a lawyer who has reason to believe that another lawyer may be unable to sign a certificate to raise this issue with her colleague. Law Society of Alberta, Code of Conduct, Rule 6.02(1) (“A lawyer must be courteous and civil and act in good faith with all persons with whom the lawyer has dealings in the course of his or her practice”). E. The Court Should Not Reward a Litigant Whose Counsel Falsely Certifies Something To Be True 63 An order granting the plaintiff indemnification from the defendant for the costs of experts' reports filed after her counsel had filed an inaccurate form 37 request would send a signal that parties can disregard court rules without the prospect of sanction. This is not a message which would promote expeditious and orderly resolution of disputes presented to this court and encourage rule compliant behaviour. 64 Denying the plaintiff her costs for the contested experts' reports is one way of recording this Court's disapproval of the conduct of her lawyer. See Grenzservice Speditions Ges. m.b.H. v. Jans, 129 D.L.R. 4th 733, 760 (B.C. Sup. Ct. 1995) (“The only way a court can express its disapproval of such egregious behaviour is by removing counsel from the record”); Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v. Wenzel, 399 A.R. 166, 171 (Q.B. 2006) (the court criticized defence counsel who misled the Court when he asserted that a requested adjournment would not adversely affect the plaintiffs when he knew that his client would use the delay to seek an anti-suit injunction in Texas) &P.S. Refson & Co. v. Saggers, [1984] 1 W.R.L. 1025, 1029 (Ch.) (court expressed dismay that counsel failed to promptly issue a writ, as promised, after securing an ex parte interim injunction for an intended plaintiff when the court registry was closed). 65 Counsel must never forget that they are officers of the court and that the judicial process demands much of them. They must always act with integrity and honour. Hutchinson v. Stephens, 48 E.R. 461, 464-65 (Ch. 1837) (“I am far from thinking that any counsel will knowingly violate or silently permit to be violated, any established rule of the court to promote the purpose of any client”). 66 Certifying something to be true when it is not is a breach of the high standard applicable to counsel for over 500 years. 67 The plaintiff must suffer for the sins of her counsel. His sins are hers. There is no reason to relieve her of this burden: Ordinarily this court should not distinguish between the litigant himself and his advisors. There are good reasons why the court should not: first, if anyone is to suffer for the failure of the solicitor it is better that it be the client rather than another party to the litigation; secondly, the disgruntled client may in appropriate circumstances have his remedies in damages or in respect of wasted costs … Hytec Information Systems Ltd. v. Coventry City Council, [1997] 1 W.L.R. 1666, 1675 (C.A. 1996). 68 Before the defendants could be held responsible for the fees linked to the contested expert reports, the plaintiff would have had to extract a promise from the defendants that they would pay the fees of experts the plaintiff had retained regardless of the date the plaintiff served their reports on the defendants. The plaintiff did not do this despite the fact defendants' counsel had signalled the position he would take on this issue in his August 2, 2012, letter to plaintiff's counsel. 2. One Needs Permission to Bring an Application after Trial is Scheduled In Signalta Resources Limited v. Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2018 ABQB 935, 2018 CarswellAlta 2904, the defendant wanted to apply for summary judgment dismissing part of the Plaintiff's claim. However, the action had already been set down for trial. The question was: did the Defendant need permission for such an application, and, if so, should the permission be granted. Justice Eamon determined that permission was required. His Lordship said: [5] The Rules do not explicitly require a party to seek permission to make an interlocutory application after a matter is scheduled for trial. The Plaintiff argues that this requirement is implicit in the Rules and that the same requirement under the former rules of court, Rule 236, AR 390/1968, continues to apply. … [14] The drafter of the Rules did not explicitly continue the limitation of former rule 236(6) into the trial scheduling system under the Rules. In VAS v Grace, 2013 ABQB 746 (CanLII), Justice Veit (as she then was) held that the limitation on further pre-trial proceedings after entry for trial continued to apply: [5] The current Rules state that parties requesting a trial date must certify that all applications related to the action have been disposed of and that no other pre-trial steps are required [Rule 8.4(3)(i)] and that proof of such certification is to be provided through Form 37. Although the Rules outline a procedure in which the parties can engage if they are unable to certify everything required by Rule 8.4(3), the parties here did, eventually, file a Form 37 certifying trial readiness. Although the wording of s. 5(d) of Form 37 is not felicitous, and does not closely track Rule 8.4(3)(i), its substantive meaning is clear: no further applications will be brought once the Form is filed. Moreover, I assume that the parties did, as required by Rule 8.7, file Form 39 confirming the trial date 3 months prior to December 2, 2013. While no current Rule clearly states that once Form 37 and Form 39 have been filed, no interlocutory applications relating to questioning may be brought without leave of the court, I have concluded that such a result is implicit in the Rules. Indeed, in Tan v Swyrd 2013 ABQB 229 (CanLII), Wakeling J. emphasizes the effect of filing Form 37 in much the same way as the Court of Appeal had dealt with the undertaking in the former certificate of readiness. In my view, although the previous explicit reference in the Rules to leave being available to initiate process after the equivalent of Form 37 had been filed is not found in the current Rules, the same approach applies, i.e. a court may give leave for an interlocutory application despite the filing of Form 37. However, some justification for departure from the Rule must be advanced; as Stevenson & Côté's Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook points out, one of the factors which a court should take into account in deciding whether it should grant leave is whether the potential for an interlocutory appeal is lost. (Underlining added) [15] In Wenzel v Nenshi, both in reasons reported at 2015 ABQB 742 (CanLII) (at paras 30 and 49), and in earlier, more extensive verbal reasons, Action No 1301-13429, November 12, 2015, Justice Gates applied the same limitation in the case of an order under Rule 8.5. He disagreed with Justice Kent's obiter dicta in Encana v ARC Resources Ltd, 2013 ABQB 96 (CanLII) at para 11 that leave was not required under the Rules. [16] CNRL argues that Rule 7.2 providing the Court may “at any time in an action” give a summary judgment excludes an implied requirement for leave. I adopt Justice Gates' answer to this argument in his verbal reasons in Wenzel cited in the preceding para, at p 6: … In my view, it does not follow from this language that leave is not required. Rather, it provides that summary judgment remains an option at any time, but it does not address the question of whether leave is required to bring a summary judgment application at a specific time, namely after a trial date has been set. … [18] Late pre-trial proceedings could, if not managed, jeopardize trial dates, significantly affect management and allocation of the Court's trial resources, distract the parties from trial preparation, and create unfairness to a party who loses its trial date or a party who may be forced to forego an interlocutory appeal to keep its trial date. Examples include pleadings amendments prompting additional pre-trial investigation or discovery, or summary judgment or Rule 3.68 applications to strike out claims which can prompt pleading amendments, changes in trial strategy or reworking of expert reports. [19] There would be little purpose in requiring certifications of readiness and completion, if the parties could continue to act as if matters were not completed. The management of the trial list for the benefit of the public would soon be undermined if parties could continue pre-hearing procedures without accountability to the Court, which is responsible for managing the list. [20] Given the certification requirements and their purpose and context, I agree with the VAS and Wenzel cases that permission to bring an interlocutory application is required after the matter is scheduled for trial, unless (I add) the Form 37 or the Order contemplated continuation of the pre-trial activity in question. As to when permission to bring an application should be granted, his Lordship said: [21] I do not accept the test suggested in some of the Ontario authorities cited in argument that a substantial and unexpected change in circumstances is required for permission to be granted. Some applications are better late than never, in order to determine the real issue in dispute. For example, an amendment to pleadings should be allowed, no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice to the other side, and even that is no obstacle if it is repaired (Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43). Generally, the application should be determined by weighing all the circumstances and deciding whether permitting the application would, as expressed in Part 1 of the Rules, “provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way”. 3. Rule applies to a signed, but unfiled, Form 37 In Benc v. Parker, 2016 ABCA 82, 2016 CarswellAlta 539, as the result of a motor vehicle accident, the plaintiff commenced a personal injury action against the defendant. Counsel for the parties completed and signed a Form 37. Defence counsel “wrote ‘not applicable’ in response to the question of whether all medical examinations and reports had been completed and exchanged.” Though the Form was signed by both counsel, it was not filed with the Court. The defendant brought an application “for an order requiring the [plaintiff] to attend for an independent medical examination. The [plaintiff] filed a cross-application pursuant to rule 8.5 for an Order to file a request to schedule a trial date in reliance upon [the] Form 37.” A Chambers judge dismissed the defendant's application and granted the plaintiff's cross-application. The plaintiff appealed and the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The Court said, at paragraphs 9–12: 9 As we see it, the disposition in the Court below is unassailable. Appellant's counsel in completing Form 37 cannot be said to have certified that medical examinations or reports under part 5, division 3 were incomplete and that such matters would be completed in a timely way. The purpose of rule 8.4 is to authorize the Clerk to fix a date for trial if the conditions precedent are met. The Clerk has no authority to do so unless Form 37 is filed. In our opinion, writing “not applicable” does not alert the Court Clerk to any deficiency so as to be satisfied that subrules (2) & (3) of rule 8.4 have been complied with, nor, if in doubt, to refer the matter to a judge for directions or decision. 10 Put another way, the purpose of the filing requirement of rule 8.4, given scarce judicial resources, is to assure that the Clerk of the Court does not set matters down for trial unless and until the parties certify that all pre-trial steps have been completed, or is satisfied that the parties will, or are likely to be ready by the proposed trial date. The rule contemplates that administrative step i.e. filing to provide the Clerk of the Court with requisite certifications and assurances that the time set aside for trial will not be squandered. 11 It does not follow, however, that a completed Form 37 that has been reviewed, signed and exchanged by the parties is of no effect. As we see it, it constitutes a binding mutual representation to the opposite party that the issues are joined and that no further steps will be taken by either party save to proceed to trial (or as otherwise disclosed). Counsel for both parties are entitled to rely upon such representations in preparation for trial and, by way of illustration, to dispense with witnesses, to pursue others, or to discard documentary evidence now thought unnecessary. That is not to say that it is incumbent upon counsel to demonstrate prejudice. On the contrary the completion of a Form 37 constitutes, in our opinion, an undertaking in the throes of litigation by one party to another that absent mutual error or unilateral mistake in completing the Form (in which case an application for relief may be brought before a judge), the plaintiff and the defendant will take no further pre-trial steps. 12 In this case, it matters not that Form 37, as completed, was not filed. Bearing as it did the signatures of both counsel, it was both relied upon by the respondent and capable of being filed. In our opinion, the applications brought by the parties in the court below, were for the reasons set out above, properly adjudicated. 4. Surrebuttal reports are governed by Rules 8.4(3)(c) and 8.5(1)(c) In Monument Machine Shop Ltd. v. Calibre Drilling Ltd., 2018 ABQB 857, 2018 CarswellAlta 2365, Justice Dario said: [26] In summary, if a surrebuttal report is to be relied upon at trial, rules 8.4(3)(c) and 8.5(1)(c) apply to such a report, and this must be taken into consideration when a Form 37, Form 38, and/or Form 39 is filed. Otherwise, to allow a late surrebuttal expert report may negate some of the intent behind the timelines set out in the Rules, including to discourage surprise and encourage settlement.

Costs for Contravention In Tan v.
Swyrd, 2013 ABQB 229, 2013 CarswellAlta 522, 560 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 369, Justice Wakeling considered the costs consequences of a plaintiff contravening Rule 8.4(3).

His Lordship said, at paragraphs 47–68: 47 Rule 8.4(3)(c) of the new rules states that a party who files a form 37 request must “certify that any expert reports have been exchanged” and that the process described in Part 5, Division 2, including questioning of experts, is complete.
Form 37 contains a signature block for counsel.
48 This rule is designed to reduce risk that a party will seek an adjournment of a trial because a necessary expert's report has not been served on another party in a timely manner.
A last minute adjournment prejudices not only the parties in the action directly affected by the adjournment but potentially other litigants whose actions are trial ready.
A trial date may never be used.
Other actions that had back-up status may settle or the counsel or witnesses may not be able to adjust their schedules on short notice.
Rule 8.4(3)(c) protects all litigants for whom a trial date is a valuable commodity.
The fact that a very small percentage of actions are ever tried does not diminish the harm the court system suffers when a trial date is not used.
49 What does “certify” mean in this context?

50 Plaintiff's counsel argued that a lawyer could file a form 37 request notwithstanding that his client had not served on the other party all the experts' reports the client intended to rely on: “Form 37 states that ‘all expert reports have been exchanged’, the [sic] fair reading of this paragraph would be that it certifies that the parties have exchanged their expert reports in their possession at the time of signing and does not as such preclude the exchange of future expert reports” (emphasis in the original).
51 This argument is unsound.
52 First, it completely disregards the ordinary meaning of “certify”. “Certify”, according to Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged
(1971), means “1: to attest esp. authoritatively or formally …
(b): to present in formal communication, esp. in a document under hand or seal …
(c): to confirm or attest often by a document under hand or seal as being true …
(d): to attest officially …”.

Combining this definition and the text of rule 8.4(3)(c) results in this conclusion: a party may file a form 37 request only if her counsel has carefully considered whether experts reports are needed and, if they are a necessary part of her client's case, she has served on the other party all the experts' reports on which the client intends to rely at trial.
A declaration that is not the product of deliberation is of no value.
53 A lawyer who signs a certificate for her client is not vouching for the veracity of the statements the other party certifies to be true.
54 Second, the argument fails to take subrules 8.4(5) and
(b) of the new Alberta Rules of Court into account … Subrules 8.4(5) and
(6) explicitly direct counsel who has not exchanged all experts' reports to notify the court clerk of this deficiency.
This information allows the court clerk to determine whether the proposed exchange time-lines are reasonable.
It is the court clerk's job to review form 37 and decide whether an action will be placed on a trial list.
The court clerk and a judge cannot make a rational decision if parties provide inaccurate information.

55 Third, the plaintiff's position fails to recognize that rule 8.4(3)(c) calls upon counsel, in an official court document, to confirm the existence of a fact, critical to the court clerk's assessment of whether an action is trial ready.
Rule 8.6 of the new rules, the provision which limits the circumstances under which a trial may be adjourned, reinforces the importance of counsel's certificate.
A lawyer is an officer of the court on whose word others in the court system must be able to rely in making important decisions.
Legal Professional Act, R.S.A.
102(2) (a Law Society member is an officer of the Court of Queen's Bench); Rondel v.
657, 665 (C.A.) (“[A]n advocate … is a minister of justice equally with the judge”); Hutchinson v.
Stephens, 48 E.R.
1837) (counsel perform “truly honourable and important services … as ministers of justice, acting in aid of the Judge before whom they practice”); A.
Scalia & B.

Garner, Making Your Case: The Art of Persuading Judges 33 (2008) (the United States Supreme Court considers a great advocate the tenth justice); Wakeling “The Oral Component of Appellate Work”, 5 Dalhousie L.J.
18 (1979) (“As an officer of the court the advocate is obliged to play a role in the law making process”) & Great Australian Gold Mining Co. v.
Martin, 7 Ch.
D.
1877) (a statement counsel signs must be accorded the “greatest possible respect”).

The Law Society of Alberta's Code of Conduct declares that this concept is fundamental, recording as its first principle that a “lawyer has a duty to carry forward on the practice of law and discharge all responsibilities to … tribunals … honourably and with integrity”.
As one would expect, the Code of Conduct appreciates that “[p]ublic confidence in the administration of justice and in the legal profession may be eroded by a lawyer's irresponsible conduct”.
Code of Conduct (2012 version).
It is not unusual for court rules to incorporate counsel's certificate into a court procedure.

For example, Form M of the Court of Appeal of Alberta's practice directions insists that counsel certify that she has “personally checked the contents of the appeal digest and found them to be complete”.
Counsel is in the best position to provide this necessary information.

Form 25B of the Rules of the Supreme Court of Canada obliges counsel to certify, in part, “whether there is, pursuant to an order or legislation, a ban on the publication of evidence or the names or identity of a party or witness”.
Again, counsel is in the best position to bring this important information to the court's attention.
In these two cases, counsel's certificate allows the court system to proceed with a high degree of comfort that foreseeable problems will not occur.
D.
Plaintiff's Counsel Was Not in a Position To Certify That All Expert Reports Had Been Served.
56 The plaintiff's counsel was not in a position to certify that all expert reports had been served when the plaintiff filed form 37.
None of the nine experts' reports which the plaintiff estimated she would introduce at trial had been served on the defendants when plaintiff's counsel signed the form 37 request.

57 The plaintiff's counsel acknowledges in his written argument the existence of the underlying facts which made it impossible to certify that the parties had exchanged all expert reports: The Plaintiff served her Opinion Statements under Rule 5.35 on June 11, 2012.
All expert reports generated to this point in time were appended to these expert reports.

When Form 37 was filed eight months prior, the Defendant knew that Rule 5.35 production had not yet occurred, and at no point insisted on strict compliance with the new rules which required this exchange to be completed before the Form could be signed and filed. … When it became clear that settlement … was not in the cards, the preparation of the 5.35 statements commenced resulting in the service of the same by June 11, 2012. … …[B]oth counsel signed Form 37, confirming that all experts reports have been exchanged, however both counsel knew at the time that the 5.35 exchange had not occurred.
(emphasis added) 58 I commend counsel for his candid concession.
59 I have not considered whether the defendants' counsel was in a position to sign form 37.
This is not an issue before me.
The defendants are not seeking from the plaintiff reimbursement for any expert fees.
But I do note that defendants' counsel asserts in his brief that “[t]he plaintiff had the Defendants' Expert reports, respectively, on January 28, 2011 and August 24, 2011”.
My review of the filed material did not confirm that the defendants served rule 5.35 experts' reports on the plaintiff on those days.
Perhaps they were not included in the record.
I did discover two service letters dated January 28, 2011 and August 24, 2011 which invoked rule 5.44 of the new Alberta Rules of Court.

60 Rule 5.44(3)(a) directs a party causing a medical examination to be conducted to “on request, deliver promptly to each of the other parties a copy of the detailed written report of the health care professional's findings and conclusions”.
By complying with rule 5.44(3)(a) a party is not serving on the other side an expert's report referred to in rules 5.34 and 5.35.
Rule 5.34 prescribes the format of an expert's report.
An expert's report must comply with Form 25 unless the parties agree to a modified format.
There is no similar requirement for a rule 5.44(3)(a) written report of a health care professional.
Good practice no doubt suggests that a rule 5.44(3)(a) report be referred and attached to a rule 5.34(a) expert's report.
61 I restate a point I made earlier.

62 A counsel who signs a form 37 request certifies that she has carefully considered what role experts will play in the proof of her client's case and that her client has served on the other party all experts' reports on which the client will rely.
Her certificate does not reflect her assessment of whether other counsel is in a position to sign a comparable certificate.
In some circumstances, professional courtesy may cause a lawyer who has reason to believe that another lawyer may be unable to sign a certificate to raise this issue with her colleague.

Law Society of Alberta, Code of Conduct, Rule 6.02(1) (“A lawyer must be courteous and civil and act in good faith with all persons with whom the lawyer has dealings in the course of his or her practice”).
E.

The Court Should Not Reward a Litigant Whose Counsel Falsely Certifies Something To Be True 63 An order granting the plaintiff indemnification from the defendant for the costs of experts' reports filed after her counsel had filed an inaccurate form 37 request would send a signal that parties can disregard court rules without the prospect of sanction.
This is not a message which would promote expeditious and orderly resolution of disputes presented to this court and encourage rule compliant behaviour.
64 Denying the plaintiff her costs for the contested experts' reports is one way of recording this Court's disapproval of the conduct of her lawyer.
See Grenzservice Speditions Ges. m.b.H. v.
Jans, 129 D.L.R.
Sup.
Ct.
1995) (“The only way a court can express its disapproval of such egregious behaviour is by removing counsel from the record”); Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel, 399 A.R.

2006) (the court criticized defence counsel who misled the Court when he asserted that a requested adjournment would not adversely affect the plaintiffs when he knew that his client would use the delay to seek an anti-suit injunction in Texas) &P.S.
Refson & Co. v.
Saggers, [1984] 1 W.R.L.

1025, 1029 (Ch.) (court expressed dismay that counsel failed to promptly issue a writ, as promised, after securing an ex parte interim injunction for an intended plaintiff when the court registry was closed).
65 Counsel must never forget that they are officers of the court and that the judicial process demands much of them.
They must always act with integrity and honour.
Hutchinson v.
Stephens, 48 E.R.
1837) (“I am far from thinking that any counsel will knowingly violate or silently permit to be violated, any established rule of the court to promote the purpose of any client”).
66 Certifying something to be true when it is not is a breach of the high standard applicable to counsel for over 500 years.
67 The plaintiff must suffer for the sins of her counsel.
His sins are hers.
There is no reason to relieve her of this burden: Ordinarily this court should not distinguish between the litigant himself and his advisors.

There are good reasons why the court should not: first, if anyone is to suffer for the failure of the solicitor it is better that it be the client rather than another party to the litigation; secondly, the disgruntled client may in appropriate circumstances have his remedies in damages or in respect of wasted costs … Hytec Information Systems Ltd. v.
Coventry City Council, [1997] 1 W.L.R.

68 Before the defendants could be held responsible for the fees linked to the contested expert reports, the plaintiff would have had to extract a promise from the defendants that they would pay the fees of experts the plaintiff had retained regardless of the date the plaintiff served their reports on the defendants.
The plaintiff did not do this despite the fact defendants' counsel had signalled the position he would take on this issue in his August 2, 2012, letter to plaintiff's counsel.
One Needs Permission to Bring an Application after Trial is Scheduled In Signalta Resources Limited v.
Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2018 ABQB 935, 2018 CarswellAlta 2904, the defendant wanted to apply for summary judgment dismissing part of the Plaintiff's claim.
However, the action had already been set down for trial.
The question was: did the Defendant need permission for such an application, and, if so, should the permission be granted.
Justice Eamon determined that permission was required.
His Lordship said: [5] The Rules do not explicitly require a party to seek permission to make an interlocutory application after a matter is scheduled for trial.

The Plaintiff argues that this requirement is implicit in the Rules and that the same requirement under the former rules of court, Rule 236, AR 390/1968, continues to apply. … [14] The drafter of the Rules did not explicitly continue the limitation of former rule 236(6) into the trial scheduling system under the Rules.

In VAS v Grace, 2013 ABQB 746 (CanLII), Justice Veit (as she then was) held that the limitation on further pre-trial proceedings after entry for trial continued to apply: [5] The current Rules state that parties requesting a trial date must certify that all applications related to the action have been disposed of and that no other pre-trial steps are required [Rule 8.4(3)(i)] and that proof of such certification is to be provided through Form 37.

Although the Rules outline a procedure in which the parties can engage if they are unable to certify everything required by Rule 8.4(3), the parties here did, eventually, file a Form 37 certifying trial readiness.
Although the wording of s.
5(d) of Form 37 is not felicitous, and does not closely track Rule 8.4(3)(i), its substantive meaning is clear: no further applications will be brought once the Form is filed.
Moreover, I assume that the parties did, as required by Rule 8.7, file Form 39 confirming the trial date 3 months prior to December 2, 2013.

While no current Rule clearly states that once Form 37 and Form 39 have been filed, no interlocutory applications relating to questioning may be brought without leave of the court, I have concluded that such a result is implicit in the Rules.

Indeed, in Tan v Swyrd 2013 ABQB 229 (CanLII), Wakeling J. emphasizes the effect of filing Form 37 in much the same way as the Court of Appeal had dealt with the undertaking in the former certificate of readiness.

In my view, although the previous explicit reference in the Rules to leave being available to initiate process after the equivalent of Form 37 had been filed is not found in the current Rules, the same approach applies, i.e. a court may give leave for an interlocutory application despite the filing of Form 37.

However, some justification for departure from the Rule must be advanced; as Stevenson & Côté's Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook points out, one of the factors which a court should take into account in deciding whether it should grant leave is whether the potential for an interlocutory appeal is lost.

(Underlining added) [15] In Wenzel v Nenshi, both in reasons reported at 2015 ABQB 742 (CanLII) (at paras 30 and 49), and in earlier, more extensive verbal reasons, Action No 1301-13429, November 12, 2015, Justice Gates applied the same limitation in the case of an order under Rule 8.5.
He disagreed with Justice Kent's obiter dicta in Encana v ARC Resources Ltd, 2013 ABQB 96 (CanLII) at para 11 that leave was not required under the Rules.
[16] CNRL argues that Rule 7.2 providing the Court may “at any time in an action” give a summary judgment excludes an implied requirement for leave.
I adopt Justice Gates' answer to this argument in his verbal reasons in Wenzel cited in the preceding para, at p 6: … In my view, it does not follow from this language that leave is not required.

Rather, it provides that summary judgment remains an option at any time, but it does not address the question of whether leave is required to bring a summary judgment application at a specific time, namely after a trial date has been set. … [18] Late pre-trial proceedings could, if not managed, jeopardize trial dates, significantly affect management and allocation of the Court's trial resources, distract the parties from trial preparation, and create unfairness to a party who loses its trial date or a party who may be forced to forego an interlocutory appeal to keep its trial date.

Examples include pleadings amendments prompting additional pre-trial investigation or discovery, or summary judgment or Rule 3.68 applications to strike out claims which can prompt pleading amendments, changes in trial strategy or reworking of expert reports.
[19] There would be little purpose in requiring certifications of readiness and completion, if the parties could continue to act as if matters were not completed.

The management of the trial list for the benefit of the public would soon be undermined if parties could continue pre-hearing procedures without accountability to the Court, which is responsible for managing the list.

[20] Given the certification requirements and their purpose and context, I agree with the VAS and Wenzel cases that permission to bring an interlocutory application is required after the matter is scheduled for trial, unless (I add) the Form 37 or the Order contemplated continuation of the pre-trial activity in question.

As to when permission to bring an application should be granted, his Lordship said: [21] I do not accept the test suggested in some of the Ontario authorities cited in argument that a substantial and unexpected change in circumstances is required for permission to be granted.
Some applications are better late than never, in order to determine the real issue in dispute.

For example, an amendment to pleadings should be allowed, no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice to the other side, and even that is no obstacle if it is repaired (Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43).

Generally, the application should be determined by weighing all the circumstances and deciding whether permitting the application would, as expressed in Part 1 of the Rules, “provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way”.
Rule applies to a signed, but unfiled, Form 37 In Benc v.
Parker, 2016 ABCA 82, 2016 CarswellAlta 539, as the result of a motor vehicle accident, the plaintiff commenced a personal injury action against the defendant.
Counsel for the parties completed and signed a Form 37.

Defence counsel “wrote ‘not applicable’ in response to the question of whether all medical examinations and reports had been completed and exchanged.” Though the Form was signed by both counsel, it was not filed with the Court.
The defendant brought an application “for an order requiring the [plaintiff] to attend for an independent medical examination.

The [plaintiff] filed a cross-application pursuant to rule 8.5 for an Order to file a request to schedule a trial date in reliance upon [the] Form 37.” A Chambers judge dismissed the defendant's application and granted the plaintiff's cross-application.

The Clerk has no authority to do so unless Form 37 is filed.
In our opinion, writing “not applicable” does not alert the Court Clerk to any deficiency so as to be satisfied that subrules
(3) of rule 8.4 have been complied with, nor, if in doubt, to refer the matter to a judge for directions or decision.

10 Put another way, the purpose of the filing requirement of rule 8.4, given scarce judicial resources, is to assure that the Clerk of the Court does not set matters down for trial unless and until the parties certify that all pre-trial steps have been completed, or is satisfied that the parties will, or are likely to be ready by the proposed trial date.
The rule contemplates that administrative step i.e. filing to provide the Clerk of the Court with requisite certifications and assurances that the time set aside for trial will not be squandered.
11 It does not follow, however, that a completed Form 37 that has been reviewed, signed and exchanged by the parties is of no effect.

As we see it, it constitutes a binding mutual representation to the opposite party that the issues are joined and that no further steps will be taken by either party save to proceed to trial (or as otherwise disclosed).

Counsel for both parties are entitled to rely upon such representations in preparation for trial and, by way of illustration, to dispense with witnesses, to pursue others, or to discard documentary evidence now thought unnecessary.
That is not to say that it is incumbent upon counsel to demonstrate prejudice.

On the contrary the completion of a Form 37 constitutes, in our opinion, an undertaking in the throes of litigation by one party to another that absent mutual error or unilateral mistake in completing the Form (in which case an application for relief may be brought before a judge), the plaintiff and the defendant will take no further pre-trial steps.
12 In this case, it matters not that Form 37, as completed, was not filed.
Bearing as it did the signatures of both counsel, it was both relied upon by the respondent and capable of being filed.
In our opinion, the applications brought by the parties in the court below, were for the reasons set out above, properly adjudicated.
Surrebuttal reports are governed by Rules 8.4(3)(c) and 8.5(1)(c) In Monument Machine Shop Ltd. v.

Calibre Drilling Ltd., 2018 ABQB 857, 2018 CarswellAlta 2365, Justice Dario said: [26] In summary, if a surrebuttal report is to be relied upon at trial, rules 8.4(3)(c) and 8.5(1)(c) apply to such a report, and this must be taken into consideration when a Form 37, Form 38, and/or Form 39 is filed.

paragraphs.text: (1) On application by a party in Form 38, the judge may set a trial date or direct the court clerk to do so if (a) the judge (i) is satisfied that the parties have participated in at least one of the dispute resolution processes described in rule 4.16(1), (ii) has granted an order under rule 4.16(2) waiving the dispute resolution process requirement, or (iii) grants an order under rule 4.16(2) in the course of an application under this rule, (b) the judge has all the information described in rule 8.4(2) except the certifications referred to in rule 8.4(2)(e), (c) with respect to the certification of matters referred to in rule 8.4(3), the judge (i) receives the necessary certifications, (ii) has sufficient information to schedule a trial date without one or more certifications, or (iii) gives directions as required and is satisfied that a trial date should be set, and (d) the judge is satisfied that the parties will or are likely to be ready for trial by the proposed trial date. (2) Subject to rule 1.5(4), the Court may make any procedural order to expedite or facilitate activities necessary to meet or to obtain a trial date. (3) An order may be made under subrule (2) despite the fact that the parties (a) have signed a Form 37 or Form 38, or (b) have complied with rule 8.4(3). Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 13; 36/2020, s. 8

sentences.text: Notice of trial date

paragraphs.text: (1) When the court clerk or the judge sets a trial date, the court clerk must give notice to every party of the date, place and duration set for the trial. (2) A trial for which a trial date has been scheduled may not be adjourned or abandoned unless (a) a notice of discontinuance of the action has been filed, (b) a memorandum of settlement of the action, signed by the parties, has been filed, or (c) the judge permits. (3) A trial date and the period of time scheduled for the trial may be changed only with the judge's permission. (4) Subrules (2) and (3) apply whether or not the parties consent to an adjournment or to a change in the duration of the trial. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 14

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.6:1 Rule 8.6 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.6. In Lameman v. Alberta, 2011 ABQB 40, 2011 CarswellAlta 117, Justice Yamauchi set out the following factors which should be considered when determining whether an adjournment of a trial should be granted: [33] From the following cases, one can see that a court might consider the following factors when considering whether it should exercise its discretion to grant an adjournment: 1. courts should make a just determination of the real matters in dispute and they should decide cases on their merits; 2. the prejudice caused by granting or denying the adjournment; 3. the applicant’s explanation for not being ready to proceed; 4. the length of the adjournment the applicant is seeking and the consequent disruption of the court’s schedule; 5. the importance of effectively enforcing previous court orders; 6. the proper marshalling of evidence and prosecution of complex and multi-faceted actions; 7. whether there is a realistic expectation that the adjournment will accomplish its stated purpose; 8. the history of the proceedings, including other adjournments and delays, and at whose instance those adjournments and delays occurred; 9. where a party is seeking the adjournment to amend pleadings, how long counsel has known of the issue to which the amendment is aimed and whether counsel has had previous opportunities to amend; 10. whether the application is merely an attempt to delay the proceedings; and 11. the party who seeks the adjournment should not bear the consequences of its counsel’s failures.

Out-of-province Witnesses Remember to use the provisions of the Interprovincial Subpoena Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. I-8.1, s. 5: 5. (1) Where a party to a proceeding in a court in Alberta causes a subpoena to be issued for service in another province, the party may attend on a judge of the Court of Queen's Bench, who (a) shall hear and examine the party or the party's counsel, if any, and (b) on being satisfied that the attendance in Alberta of the person required in Alberta as a witness (i) is necessary for the due adjudication of the proceeding in which the subpoena has been issued, and (ii) in relation to the nature and importance of the proceedings, is reasonable and essential to the due administration of justice in Alberta, shall sign a certificate in the prescribed form and shall cause the certificate to be impressed with the seal of the Court of Queen's Bench. (2) The certificate referred to in subsection (1) shall be either attached to or endorsed on the subpoena. 2. Does Not Apply to Discoveries I am of the view that the legislature intended s. 5 of the Act to allow witnesses to be brought from out of province to testify in court. My view is drawn from the words used in the section. I find the words “is necessary for the due adjudication of the proceeding”, used in subs. (b)(1) combined with the introductory language “a proceeding in court” convince me of this. I am also guided by the British Columbia court's interpretation of their Act. Further, the definition in the Act of “court in Alberta” includes a board, commission, tribunal or other body. Of the examples given the process takes place in the presence of the adjudicator. Therefore, I find I am persuaded the powers under the Act do not extend to discovery process. Cambridge (Next Friend of) v. Traff (1994), 19 Alta. L.R. (3d) 248 (Q.B.) at 253, per Smith, J. This decision was referred to with approval by Belzil J. in Mathes-Porter v. Forden (1998), 242 A.R. 351 (Q.B.), at 353, and by Clarke J. in WIC Premium Television Ltd. v. General Instrument Corp. (1999), 243 A.R. 324 at 327 (Q.B.). 3. Subpoena Duces Tecum In Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1990), 78 Alta. L.R. (2d) 207 (Q.B.), at 209, Berger J. stated: A subpoena duces tecum (to produce documents) or a writ ad testificandum (to appear and testify) may be issued by a party to proceedings to a witness who is not a party. In Amey v. Long (1808), 103 E.R. 653, the nature of a subpoena duces tecum was described as follows: The writ of subpoena duces tecum is of compulsory obligation on a witness to produce papers thereby demanded which he has in his possession, and which he has no lawful or reasonable excuse for withholding; of the validity of which excuse the Court, and not the witness, is to judge. In Alberta the procedure is set out in R. 293 of the Rules of Court … A witness served with a subpoena who is not a party to the cause of action has, however, the status to move to have the subpoena quashed: Steel v. Savoury (1891), 8 T.L.R. 94 at 95: In a position like the present a witness is entitled to come to the Court at once, and was not bound to stand by and wait till some motion for attachment was made or other proceeding taken against him for non-compliance with the subpoena. A subpoena, properly served and correct in form, may be quashed where it is held to be either irrelevant, oppressive, or an abuse of the process of the court: Senior v. Holdsworth, [1975] 2 All E.R. 1009 (C.A.). In proceedings to quash a subpoena duces tecum, the onus is on the attacker of the subpoena in moving to set it aside: Fort Norman Explor. Inc. v. McLauchlin (1982), 36 O.R. (2d) 787 (H.C.). Reid J. stated in Fort Norman, at p. 790: Since Canada Metal makes it clear that the mere attack itself casts no onus upon the issuer of the subpoena to justify its issue, the onus lies upon the attacker. If the ground is abuse it is not for the issuer of the subpoena to show no abuse: it is for the attacker to show an abuse. There is, however, a method by which a party to an action can initiate discovery of documents of a non-party. [The court then referred to R. 209(1)]. Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1990), 78 Alta. L.R. (2d) 207 at 209, 212 (Q.B.).

paragraphs.text: 8.10. Order of presentation
paragraphs.heading: Part 8. Trial

sentences.text: Order of presentation

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the Court directs otherwise, the order of presentation at a trial is as follows: (a) the plaintiff may make one opening statement and, subject to clause (b), must then adduce evidence; (b) the defendant may make one opening statement either immediately after the plaintiff's opening statement and before the plaintiff adduces evidence or at the conclusion of the plaintiff's evidence; (c) when the plaintiff's evidence is concluded, the defendant may make an opening statement if the defendant has not already done so immediately after the plaintiff's opening statement, and the defendant must then adduce evidence, if any; (d) when the defendant's evidence is concluded, the plaintiff may adduce evidence, if any, to rebut the defendant's evidence; (e) when the defendant's evidence and the plaintiff's rebuttal evidence, if any, are concluded, the plaintiff may make a closing statement, followed by the defendant's closing statement, after which the plaintiff may reply; (f) if the defendant adduces no evidence after the conclusion of the plaintiff's evidence, the plaintiff may make a closing statement, followed by the defendant's closing statement, after which the plaintiff may reply. (2) If the burden of proof for all matters in issue in the action is on the defendant, the judge may direct a different order of presentation. (3) If there are 2 or more plaintiffs or 2 or more defendants separately represented, the judge must determine the order of presentation.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.12:1 Rule 8.12 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.12. In R. v. Lindsay, 2019 ABQB 372, 2019 CarswellAlta 975, an order excluding witnesses was made. Defence counsel sought an exemption from the order for an expert who was going to be called to testify for the defence. In the course of ruling on that application, Justice Lema commented on Rule 8.12: [8] The Rules do not address the exclusion of expert witnesses specifically. [9] In its general overview of civil litigation, the Legal Education Society of Alberta says this about witness exclusion: Rule 8.12 of the Rules of Court allows the court to exclude witnesses (other than a party who may be called as a witness) from the courtroom until they have given their evidence. The practice of exclusion of witnesses has become so common that even where such an order is not given, witnesses who have not yet testified should be excluded unless specific permission of the court is granted. Where witnesses are excluded, they should not be informed of testimony given before their own testimony (Law Society of Alberta Code of Conduct, r 5.1-2(q)).[3] D. — Rationales for excluding witnesses [10] The rationales for witness exclusion generally are explored in The Law of Evidence in Canada:[4] In both civil and criminal proceedings, the trial judge has discretionary power to exclude witnesses from the courtroom until such time as it is necessary for them to give their evidence. … Upon the request of the party, the judge will, as a matter of course, grant such an order. The purpose of excluding witnesses is to preserve a witness' testimony in its original sate. A witness listening to the evidence given by another may be influenced by the latter's testimony and, accordingly, change his or her evidence to conform with it. Also, by being present in the courtroom and listening to testimony prior to giving evidence, he or she may be able to anticipate, and thereby reduce the effectiveness of, the cross-examination that will ultimately be faced. It may also facilitate collusion by allowing a witness to tailor the evidence to fit that of another. An ord4er excluding witnesses seeks to eliminate this potential unfairness. Moreover, exclusion of the witnesses may reveal earlier collusion. The similarity of language and phrases used may expose the fact that the witnesses had compared their version of events and memorized consistent stories.[5] [11] That analysis goes on to discuss the discretion to exclude parties in certain circumstances and the effect of a breach of an exclusion order, but it does not address the particular issue of excluding expert witnesses. E. — Whether those rationales apply equally to expert witnesses Civil context [12] Justice Veit examined this question in Hamblin v Ben[6][2003 ABQB 459], a motor-vehicle accident case. She held that expert witnesses constitute a separate category and should accordingly be treated differently for exclusion purposes: … expert witnesses are in a slightly different category than witness called to give original evidence to establish facts. Experts are subject to ethical standards which do not apply to other witnesses. Even more importantly, as opposed to other witnesses, experts should be assessing all of the facts with an open mind. … The experts can be in the courtroom when other witnesses are giving evidence because the experts should be basing their opinions on the actual evidence before the court; they must therefore be in a position to hear the evidence which the court hears. The check and balance on such exceptional access is that experts are required to modify their opinion according to the evidence which they hear. [7] [13] A similar analysis and end result are found in Hurst v Munch[8][2012 ONSC 6592], where Healey J. addressed whether one defendant's expert could be present in the courtroom during the testimony of another defendant's expert. A general witness-exclusion order had been made at the start of the trial, and an exception was being sought. [14] Healey J noted: [The applying defendant's counsel] relies on the direction given in Ferguson J.'s text, Ontario Courtroom Procedure, 2009 edition, at page 350, as follows: As noted below in the section E.2, because experts typically give opinions on assumed facts or fixed information, there is less concern about them being present during the testimony of other witnesses even if there is an order excluding witnesses. Experts are often exempted from an order excluding witnesses so they can assist counsel to understand the testimony and opinions of other witnesses. This also allows them to respond to the opinion of other experts and to base their own opinions on the evidence called in the trial. Therefore, it is often important for counsel to know when an opponent's expert is going to testify as they may wish to have their experts attend to listen to the testimony. So, typically, experts are exempt from exclusion orders because there is little risk that they will tailor their evidence, since experts are not the ones providing facts and therefore their credibility is not usually at issue. This rationale was discussed in Auto Workers' Village (St. Catharines) Ltd. v. Blaney, McMurtry, Stapells, Friedman (1997), 1997 CanLII 12264 (ON SC), 35 O.R. (3d) 29 (Ont.Ct.(Gen.Div.)) at page 4: The obvious rationale behind [the witness-exclusion rule] is the fear that a witness will tailor his or her testimony based on evidence heard in court. This fear is not nearly as predominant with experts (who do not speak to facts) as it is with laypersons. Experts give opinions based upon facts; they do not create the facts upon which their opinions are founded. However, an expert might be more aware than counsel regarding the importance, or lack thereof, of a given fact. An expert, therefore, could be of great assistance in suggesting to counsel questions to be put to witnesses both in-chief and in cross-examination. An expert could grasp a subtle factual distinction that arises in the evidence which might otherwise might elude counsel.

[7] [13] A similar analysis and end result are found in Hurst v Munch[8][2012 ONSC 6592], where Healey J. addressed whether one defendant's expert could be present in the courtroom during the testimony of another defendant's expert.
A general witness-exclusion order had been made at the start of the trial, and an exception was being sought.

[14] Healey J noted: [The applying defendant's counsel] relies on the direction given in Ferguson J.'s text, Ontario Courtroom Procedure, 2009 edition, at page 350, as follows: As noted below in the section E.2, because experts typically give opinions on assumed facts or fixed information, there is less concern about them being present during the testimony of other witnesses even if there is an order excluding witnesses.
Experts are often exempted from an order excluding witnesses so they can assist counsel to understand the testimony and opinions of other witnesses.
This also allows them to respond to the opinion of other experts and to base their own opinions on the evidence called in the trial.
Therefore, it is often important for counsel to know when an opponent's expert is going to testify as they may wish to have their experts attend to listen to the testimony.

So, typically, experts are exempt from exclusion orders because there is little risk that they will tailor their evidence, since experts are not the ones providing facts and therefore their credibility is not usually at issue.
This rationale was discussed in Auto Workers' Village (St.
Catharines) Ltd. v.
Blaney, McMurtry, Stapells, Friedman (1997), 1997 CanLII 12264 (ON SC), 35 O.R.
(3d) 29 (Ont.Ct.(Gen.Div.)) at page 4: The obvious rationale behind [the witness-exclusion rule] is the fear that a witness will tailor his or her testimony based on evidence heard in court.
This fear is not nearly as predominant with experts (who do not speak to facts) as it is with laypersons.
Experts give opinions based upon facts; they do not create the facts upon which their opinions are founded.
However, an expert might be more aware than counsel regarding the importance, or lack thereof, of a given fact.
An expert, therefore, could be of great assistance in suggesting to counsel questions to be put to witnesses both in-chief and in cross-examination.
An expert could grasp a subtle factual distinction that arises in the evidence which might otherwise might elude counsel.
