paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.14:1 Rule 8.14 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.14. 1. The Rule Reverses the Previous Case Law under the Old Rules In Empson v. Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 2013 ABCA 418, 2013 CarswellAlta 2418, 566 A.R. 134, 6 Alta. L.R. (6th) 414, 597 W.A.C. 134, the Court said: [4]… R. 8.14, … now allows a party to make use of transcripts from the questioning of its own witness when the witness has died. … This rule … reverses earlier case law holding that a party could not make use of its own transcripts: Paquin v. Gainers (1989) 71 Alta LR (2d) 74, 101 AR 290 (CA); Megatrend Holdings Inc. v. Glenbow-Alberta Institute, 2008 ABCA 236, 433 AR 203. In Peppler Estate v. Lee, 2019 ABQB 144, 2019 CarswellAlta 365, the plaintiff died before the medical malpractice action he brought against one of his attending physicians went to trial. An application was brought to “introduce a partly redacted transcript of Mr. Peppler's Questioning evidence under r 8.14”. Justice Topolniski said: [64] The plaintiff sought to introduce a partly redacted transcript of Mr. Peppler's Questioning evidence under r 8.14 of the Alberta Rules of Court and the reasoning in DD v Wong. I allowed the evidence to be entered, subject to my reserved ruling on its admissibility and, if admitted, the ultimate reliability. [65] For the reasons that follow, I find that the proposed Questioning evidence satisfies the requirements of r 8.14 and is properly admissible. Given significant reliability problems, little, if any, weight can be given to Mr. Peppler's uncorroborated statements, his statements that are inconsistent with the documentary evidence (assuming that documentary evidence is admissible and reliable as discussed below), his internally inconsistent statements, and his evidence that was vague and subject to uncertain memory. [66] Rule 8.14 provides that a judge may permit a party to read into evidence all or part of questioning evidence if the person so questioned is dead, to the extent that evidence would be admissible if the person were giving evidence in Court. Subsection 2 of r 8.14 provides that before deciding whether to grant permission, the judge must consider (a) the general principle that evidence should be presented orally in court, (b) how thoroughly the person was questioned under Part 5, and (c) any other appropriate factor. Further, r 8.14(3) provides that the judge may only grant permission if the facts to be proved through the questioning are important aspects of the party's case, those facts cannot be proved in any other way, and permission is restricted to the portions of the questioning related to those important facts. [67] In DD v Wong, Renke J noted that r 8.14 “can be understood as balancing the interests of examining and examined parties” by recognizing that the adverse impact on the examining parties can be offset by reading-in only what is necessary, appropriate, and fair to the examined party. Further, it is analogous to the principled exception to the hearsay rule requirements of “necessity” and “reliability.” Essentially, he argues that the Rule overrides what might otherwise be required to assess admissibility in an analysis akin to the principled exception to the hearsay rule. [68] Here, the Questioning evidence is intended to prove facts that are both important to the plaintiff's case and cannot be proved in any other way. The parties' issue is what weight, if any, should be attached to the evidence. Put another way, their concern is about ultimate reliability—whether, and to what degree, the statements should be believed and relied upon. I agree with their conclusions; however, for completeness will assess the considerations in r 8.14(2). Orality [69] The principle of orality is necessarily impacted by Mr. Peppler's death. The general principle that evidence should be presented orally in court does not weigh against admitting the proposed evidence. Thoroughness of Questioning [70] Questioning cannot delve as deeply into issues of credibility as cross-examination at trial. There is no opportunity for the trial judge to assess the witness's demeanour, tone of voice, and other observable clues relied on in assessing credibility. Accordingly, the “thoroughness of questioning” contemplated by r 8.14 cannot be interpreted as including Questioning relating to credibility. [71] Mr. Peppler's evidence was given under oath. He was skillfully questioned by Dr. Lee's counsel. While his credibility cannot be further probed by cross-examination, that does not weigh against admitting the evidence. Indeed, as Renke J observed in DD v Wong, want of cross-examination on credibility may be compensated for by judicial self-instruction and in weighing the evidence. Any Other Appropriate Factor [72] Clearly not a substitute for cross-examination in court, the Questioning procedure offers some, albeit limited, assurances concerning the assessment of Mr. Peppler's evidence. It was taken on oath and the record of the proceeding shows the interactions between Mr. Peppler and Dr. Lee's counsel. It offers some insight into Mr. Peppler's demeanor, and his forthrightness and consistency, or lack thereof. Although imperfect, this assists in assessing, if not his credibility, some indication of the reliability and consistency of his evidence. The proposed evidence is of the same provenance and shares the reliability of “read-in” evidence. 2. The Rule Does Not Cure Inadmissibility In Dame v. Wong Estate, 2018 ABQB 486, 2018 CarswellAlta 1248, 23 C.P.C. (8th) 120, the Court said: 44 Rule 8.14 authorizes the admissibility of a source of evidence, the transcript of questioning or examination for discovery. It does not cure any inadmissibility of the contents of the transcript. That is, permitting reading in does not make admissible what would not have been admissible had the proposed evidence been tendered in testimony. Under r. 8.14(1), evidence given at questioning is only admissible “to the extent that it would be admissible if the person were giving evidence in Court.” 3. The Rule Speaks in the Present Tense In Dame v. Wong Estate, 2018 ABQB 486, 2018 CarswellAlta 1248, 23 C.P.C. (8th) 120, Dr. Wong died before the trial of a medical malpractice action in which he was a defendant. The defendant's estate applied to read in at trial part of Dr. Wong's pre-trial questioning. The Plaintiffs submitted that Dr. Wong's evidence could have been preserved in another way and ought not to be admitted under R. 8.14. Justice Renke said: 58 Dr. Wong practiced until February 2014. On or about February 10, 2014, he was admitted to hospital. He was diagnosed with cancer. He remained in hospital for most of the rest of his life. He learned he was dying in April, 2014. He died on June 4, 2014. 59 The aspect of necessity at work in r. 8.14(3)(b) is whether the facts may only be proved through the Proposed Evidence or whether other sources of evidence (presumably of similar value) are available; if other another source of evidence is available, the introduction of the Proposed Evidence would not be necessary. 60 One way to put the problem under r. 8.14(3)(b) might be to ask whether the Defendants made all reasonable efforts to secure the evidence of the declarant in a manner that also preserves the rights of the other party: R v Khelawon, 2006 SCC 57, Charron J at para 104; R v Baldree, 2013 SCC 35, Fish J para 68. 61 The Plaintiffs have asserted, given the timelines, that the Defendants could have obtained an order preserving Dr. Wong's evidence while he was still alive—that is to say, an order for commission evidence or evidence de bene esse under r. 6.21. 62 On the facts as set out in Defendants' counsel's representations, the seriousness of Dr. Wong's condition was not manifest until some point in April 2014. He died June 4, 2014. There was, then, only about a month following the terminal diagnosis and death that would have permitted an examination on an urgent basis. I observe that the time from the terminal diagnosis until death would not reasonably have supported the taking of de bene esse evidence. 63 If the prospect of a de bene esse examination should have been considered after the cancer diagnosis in February, 2014, that left less than 4 months to complete the examination. 64 There was no evidence about the state of Dr. Wong's physical or psychological health as he approached death, so I cannot draw a conclusion about what would have been the last practical date for such an examination—that date would likely have passed some time before June 4, but how much before I cannot say. An examination was no doubt possible sometime after February 4 and before June 4, but when in that period I cannot say. 65 All of this is to say that I did not have the evidence before me permitting me to make a finding as to whether an order would have been granted under r. 6.21 or whether if an order were granted whether evidence could have been taken from Dr. Wong before he died. 66 I note that r. 8.14(3)(b) is in the present tense (“cannot be proved”) and in fact there is now no source of evidence other than the Proposed Evidence addressing the matters in the Proposed Evidence. The language of r. 8.14(3)(b) therefore suggests that the r. 8.14 decision is to be made given the evidence that does exist not based on evidence that might have existed. Justice Graesser commented in Brennenstuhl Estate v Trynchy, 2007 ABQB 647 at para 36 that “[w]here the witness has died without being examined de bene esse, for example, resort to prior statements or testimony is clearly necessary, as that witness's evidence cannot be obtained in any other way.” This, I note, was not a r. 8.14 case and r. 8.14 would have permitted consideration of other currently available evidence. 67 I find that the facts addressed in the Proposed Evidence cannot be proved in any other manner now. 68 I find that an examination de bene esse could not have reasonably been conducted after Dr. Wong was notified of his imminent death. 69 It is possible that an examination de bene esse could have been conducted after Dr. Wong first went to hospital. The evidence permits no definite conclusions. The Defendants, though, bear the burden of proof on this issue as proponents of the admissibility of the Proposed Evidence under r. 8.14. 70 Nonetheless, no examination de bene esse occurred. The test under r. 8.14(3)(b) is not whether the evidence could have been gathered in some other way, but whether the facts “cannot be proved in some other manner.” In this case, the relevant facts cannot be proved except through the Proposed Evidence. 71 The Defendants have satisfied the mandatory conditions of r. 8.14(3). 72 The failure to attend to an examination under r. 6.21 is relevant, nonetheless, under r. 8.14(2)(c). What “could have been” may be a consideration under r. 8.14(2)(c) (“any other appropriate factor”).

paragraphs.text: 8.15. Notice of persons not intended to be called as witnesses
paragraphs.heading: Part 8. Trial

sentences.text: Notice of persons not intended to be called as witnesses

paragraphs.text: (1) When an adverse inference might be drawn from the failure of a party to call a person as a witness, that party may serve on every other party a notice of the names of those persons that the party does not intend to call as witnesses. (2) The notice must be served one month or more before the date the trial is scheduled to start. (3) The party on whom the notice is served may serve on the party who served the notice, within 10 days after service of the notice, a statement setting out any objection to the intention not to call a person as a witness. (4) If the party on whom the notice is served does not respond to the notice of intention not to call a person as a witness, the failure to call that person as a witness is not to be considered to be adverse to the case of the party who served the notice. (5) When a party objects to the notice of intention not to call a person, the cost of calling that person as a witness must be paid by the party who objects, regardless of the result of the claim, issue or question, unless the Court decides that the objection is reasonable.

Adverse Inferences For a summary of the law on when an adverse inference may be drawn, see: KY v. Bahler, 2023 ABKB 280, 2023 CarswellAlta 1156, at paragraphs 54-56. Purpose of Rule Prior to the enactment of this Rule, counsel often had a difficult decision to make with respect to the calling of witnesses. A witness might not be necessary to prove the case, but a party might call that witness just to avoid the risk of an adverse inference. If a witness was not called, the opposing party might be tempted to request an adverse inference, even if the witness was of minimal importance. This sometimes resulted in witnesses being called that no one really wanted, thereby lengthening trials. The Rule is designed to provide a mechanism to help the parties identify which witnesses are really needed for the trial, and which can be safely excluded. The Rule itself does not create any adverse inference; it states that it applies “when, in law, an adverse inference might be drawn”. Wade v. Baxter (2001), 98 Alta. L.R. (3d) 230 (Q.B.) at 239, per Slatter J.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.16:1 Rule 8.16 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.16. Number of experts 1. What to consider on an application to permit additional experts In Smith v. Obuck, 2018 ABQB 849, 2018 CarswellAlta 3009, 2018 CarswellAlta 3009, the plaintiff in a personal injury action made an application for an order permitting the plaintiff to call “more than one physiatrist to give expert evidence at trial.” Justice Yungwirth granted the application, and set out certain questions which should be addressed by a court faced with such an application: [9] The collision that the Plaintiff alleges caused his injuries, occurred in November of 2007, some 11 years ago. Dr. Naidu, a doctor of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, saw the Plaintiff on November 1, 2011 and provided a medical-legal report dated December 22, 2011. [10] Dr. Irvine, also a doctor of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, saw the Plaintiff on January 8, 2015 and provided his medical-legal report on March 10, 2015. [11] The Plaintiff intends to call Dr. Irvine as an expert witness at trial, but would also like to call Dr. Naidu as an expert witness. … [17] Putting limitations on the number of experts that may be called at trial, appears to have a long history. I also note that though the Alberta Evidence Act no longer limits the number of expert witnesses (leaving that to the Rules), the Canada Evidence Act continues to have a limitation for expert witnesses. [18] The purpose of this type of limitation appears to be to prevent the abuse, expense, and delay caused by the excessive use of expert evidence where unnecessary to assist the Court in arriving at a just result. [19] Especially in these times of limited judicial resources, it is more important than it ever has been for the Court to limit procedures that waste those resources. [20] However, this must be weighed and balanced against the right of the Plaintiff to put its best case forward [21] After considering the arguments of both parties and the cases provided by both parties, I have concluded that in considering whether leave should be granted for Dr. Naidu to also testify, the Court must consider the following questions: 1. Is the testimony of Dr. Naidu relevant to the subject matter in issue? As causation is in issue and as 11 years have passed since the collision, the Plaintiff's medical and non-medical evidence about his condition over those 11 years and its connection to the collision, is relevant; 2. Can calling both experts be considered “piling on” or duplicative? As both experts saw the Plaintiff at different time periods following the collision, there will be aspects of their evidence that are different. There may be some duplication, but this does not appear to be a case of “piling on”; 3. Does the evidence of Dr. Naidu add anything to the evidence of Dr. Irvine? Though this cannot be fully answered without hearing the evidence of both doctors, it appears at this point that the evidence of Dr. Naidu will add something to the overall evidence in terms of the status of the Plaintiff 4 years following the collision. Dr. Irvine did not see the Plaintiff until 8 years following the collision. The Court is also concerned that if Dr. Irvine relied in any way on the report of Dr. Naidu, it may be necessary for Dr. Naidu to be called to establish the proper foundation for Dr. Irvine's opinion. If the Plaintiff is not granted leave to call Dr. Naidu at trial, there may be a delay caused if it is determined at trial that his evidence is required; 4. Is the evidence of Dr. Naidu required to allow the Plaintiff to fairly present its case? It appears from the submissions of Counsel for the Plaintiff that the Plaintiff wishes to have some continuity in the evidence in terms of his condition over the past 11 years. Refusing to allow the Plaintiff to call Dr. Naidu will have a negative impact on the Plaintiff's ability to do so and may prevent the Plaintiff from putting his best case forward; 5. Will the evidence of Dr. Naidu assist the trial judge? I find that the evidence of Dr. Naidu will most likely assist the trial judge, given that causation is in issue and given the lengthy amount of time that has passed since the collision; 6. Is allowing Dr. Naidu to testify prejudicial to the Defendant? There is no evidence that allowing Dr. Naidu to testify will be prejudicial to the Defendant. This is always a consideration for the Court in an application of this type; 7. Can any abuse, expense or delay that is determined to have been caused by the calling of Dr. Naidu be addressed by an award of costs at trial? I conclude that this concern can be addressed by an award of costs. I agree with the Defendant that the onus is on the Plaintiff to satisfy the Court that Dr. Naidu should be permitted to testify (in addition to Dr. Irvine) in this case. I find that the Plaintiff has discharged that burden. 2. Affidavit Evidence Not Always Required While substantive issues involving rights of parties will generally require formal evidence—viva voce or by affidavit—where the issue is procedural and can be truly described as a case management issue or a management of court time issue, such as leave under rule 218.4 to call additional expert witnesses, we are of the view that strict compliance with rules requiring affidavit evidence is not necessary. A case management judge, who is familiar with the issues, who has an opportunity of discussing matters with counsel and who has familiarized himself with reports such as the expert reports in question, may make such procedural rulings without affidavit evidence. This court will generally not interfere with the discretion of the case management judge to do so, otherwise the case management process would be rendered ineffective by formalized procedures and will fail to achieve its objectives. Alberta Central Airways Ltd. v. Progressive Air Services Ltd. (1999), 250 A.R. 160 (C.A.); additional reasons at, 2000 CarswellAlta 300 (C.A.), at 161 [A.R.], per McFadyen J.A.

sentences.text: Proving facts

paragraphs.text: (1) A fact to be proved at trial by the evidence of a witness must be proved by questioning the witness in Court unless (a) these rules or an enactment otherwise requires or permits, (b) the parties agree to that fact, or (c) the Court otherwise orders. (2) The Court may not order that a fact be proved by affidavit evidence of a witness if (a) a party, for good reason, wishes to cross-examine the witness, and (b) the witness may be required to attend the trial. (3) Evidence taken in any other action may be presented at trial but only if the party proposing to submit the evidence gives each of the other parties written notice of that party's intention 5 days or more before the trial is scheduled to start and obtains the Court's permission to submit the evidence.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.17:1 Rule 8.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.17. Use of affidavit evidence 1. Generally Rule 261(1) provides that normally facts are proven at trial through viva voce evidence. Rule 261(2) gives the trial judge discretion to permit a fact to be proven by affidavit or to permit an affidavit to be read in. This must be done either before or during the trial itself. The rule then limits this discretion by providing that such orders shall not be made where the other party bona fide desires to cross-examine a witness who could be produced. In other jurisdictions similar rules have been interpreted in such a manner to indicate that the proper practice is to bring an application for leave to read an affidavit as evidence before the trial: Rae v. Rae, [1924] 3 W.W.R. 446 (Sask. C.A.); Rzani v. Rzani, [1950] 2 W.W.R. 73 (Sask. C.A.). However, in both of these uncontested divorce cases exceptions were made and the affidavits were considered because of special circumstances. I can find no special circumstances in this case for reading from the affidavit because the absence of the affiant was not satisfactorily explained. I am also satisfied that the solicitor for the applicant would have a bona fide desire to cross-examine any other of the affiants who were not called as witnesses. In Ontario, proof of any fact at trial by means of affidavit without a motion for an order by the judge is considered irregular: Parker v. Parker, [1948] O.W.N. 834 (H.C.); Thorne v. Thorne, [1951] O.W.N. 545 (H.C.). Rule 261(3) has also been considered. It provides that if the matter has commenced by originating notice of motion upon any application or motion evidence may be given by affidavit unless these rules otherwise provide or the court otherwise directs. However, the use which can be made of an affidavit once it is filed is specified in R. 13, which limits the use of affidavits to applications in chambers. Since this was a trial and not a chambers application, this rule does not apply. I therefore exclude any evidence contained in the affidavits because no proper application was brought before the court to adduce affidavit evidence and the solicitor for the applicant would be denied the right to cross-examination at the trial on the material contained in the affidavit. Coronado Developments Ltd. v. W.E.D. Developments Ltd. (1982), 24 Alta. L.R. (2d) 34 (Q.B.), at 40-41, per Cawsey J. In United Inc. v. Canadian National Railway Company, 2021 ABQB 356, 2021 CarswellAlta 1102, the affiant of an affidavit died before he was cross-examined on his affidavit. The issue before Justice Rothwell was whether the affidavit could be admitted into evidence in the trial pursuant to Rule 8.17. Justice Rothwell said: [17] Both parties agree that the Hussey Affidavit is hearsay but that it can potentially be admitted if it meets the principled exception approach to hearsay, in other words, if the Affidavit is necessary and reliable: Canmore Mountain Villas Inc v Alberta (Minister of Seniors and Comunity Supports), 2010 ABQB 489 (Canmore). [18]Canmore dealt with an application to admit the affidavit evidence of Mr. Craig, a former mayor of Canmore, who had sworn an affidavit and later died. Unlike the present case, Mr. Craig had been examined on his affidavit prior to his death. [19]Canmore considered Rule 261 of the Alberta Rules of Court. Rule 8.17 is the successor to Rule 261. In Canmore, at para 26, Justice Veit held: Although the most recent principled exceptions to the hearsay rule were developed by the Supreme Court of Canada in the context of criminal law, a fortiori—that is, with even greater force—the principles apply in civil proceedings where, of course, the onus of proof is lower than in criminal proceedings. Indeed, the application of the principle has been accepted in numerous civil proceedings, including by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal: Eric Whebby Ltd. In that context, I note that the comments in Pierre relating to the criminal context in which the contemporary Canadian standard of admissibility of hearsay evidence was developed was merely intended to show that the Khan, Smith, Khelawon, etc. line of cases was merely intended to enlarge the scope of admissible hearsay, not to narrow it. [20] Justice Graesser also considered Rule 261, and followed a similar analysis, in Brennenstuhl Estate v Trynchy, 2007 ABQB 647 (Brennenstuhl Estate). … [23] In Brennenstuhl Estate Justice Graesser stated at paragraph 36: … Necessity does not require that the proponent establish that there is no other way of getting similar evidence before the court. Rather, it relates to the ability to get this particular evidence before the court. If the proposed evidence is relevant, then necessity suggests that such evidence should be before the court in its search for truth. Necessity in relation to hearsay evidence is to be considered in the context of determining whether the evidence from this witness can be obtained and admitted in some other way. Where the witness has died without being examined de bene esse, for example, resort to prior statements or testimony is clearly necessary, as that witness's evidence cannot be obtained in any other way. The fact that there is some other witness who may give similar evidence is not an answer to necessity. (Emphasis in original) [24] Justice Veit, in Canmore at para 29, relying on the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in R v B(KG), 1993 CanLII 116 (SCC), [1993] 1 SCR 740 noted that the death of a witness will, in most situations, be sufficient to meet the necessity criteria. … Reliability [28] Again both parties agree that at this stage a Court should focus on “threshold reliability” as opposed to “ultimate reliability”. Ultimate reliability will be determined at the conclusion of the trial. [29] United provided the following list of reliability factors: (a) Existence of an oath; (b) The nature of the affiant; (c) How long after the fact was the affidavit sworn; (d) The nature of the evidence; (e) The context in which the affidavit was sworn; (f) The importance of the evidence; (g) Whether the affiant had a motive to lie; (h) Whether the evidence is corroborated or appears to have a solid foundation; (i) Whether the evidence is internally inconsistent, or conflicts with other evidence; and (j) Whether there was an opportunity to cross-examine the affiant, and if so, whether there is a reasonable explanation for failing to do so. [30] These factors are drawn from Jans v Jans, 2015 SKQB 226 at para 25 (Jans). While Jans is a Saskatchewan case I accept that the above factors, while not comprehensive, are relevant considerations. … Prejudice [39] In Brennenstuhl Estate Justice Graesser relied upon the Canned Heat Marketing Inc v CFM International Inc, [1998] BCJ No. 1722 (SC) decision and held that the party opposing the affidavit's introduction bears the onus of establishing prejudice: para 24. [40] Justice Graesser adopted Master Bolton's approach, described at para 25: Master Bolton noted that the fact that disputed evidence would be admitted at trial contrary to the interests of the party opposed was not enough to establish prejudice. Instead, there must be a weighing of prejudice, because presumably the party seeking to admit the evidence will always be prejudiced if it was not allowed to present its evidence. The court is left to weigh the prejudice to each side. [41] I adopt Justice Graesser's approach. … [48] While the Hussey Affidavit can be admitted under the principled exception to the hearsay rule it still must be reviewed for compliance with the rules of evidence: Canmore at para 47. United correctly points out that evidence that would not be permitted in viva voce testimony should not be permitted by way of affidavit. … 2. Purpose of Rule … although this Rule does not specifically say so, it is my view that the Rule was intended to allow—in certain instances—a witness to give evidence in a proceeding by way of affidavit as opposed to having to appear personally and give evidence viva voce. It is not to permit an affidavit in a different matter altogether to be simply read in as proof of the contents. Heritage Freehold Specialists & Co. v. Montreal Trust Co. (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 354 (Q.B.), at p. 357, per Hawco J. 3. Timing of Application … the proper practice is to apply for leave under Rule 261(2) before the trial as opposed to at the trial. Heritage Freehold Specialists & Co. v. Montreal Trust Co. (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 354 at p. 357 (Q.B.), per Hawco J. 4. Defendant's Right to Cross-examine Co-defendant's Witnesses In Trizec Equities Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd. (1996), 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 442 (Q.B.), an action had been brought against multiple defendants. At trial, the plaintiff objected to one defendant being allowed to cross-examine witnesses called by another defendant on the ground that the defendants had cooperated in the defence of the matter. In ruling on the right to cross-examine, Mason J. said, at pp. 445-48: Counsel for Trizec are concerned because of the manifest co-operation between these Defendants in defending the action. Trizec's counsel submit that in the proceedings before this Court there has been obvious co-operation between these two Defendants. For instance, they argue that Mr. Oswald, an expert in geotechnical engineering, has been advising both Counsel for Western Caissons and Hardy with respect to geotechnical matters during trial particularly during the conduct of both Counsel's cross-examination of several of the Trizec witnesses. Counsel for Western Caissons and Hardy are alive to these concerns and acknowledge their consultations with Mr. Oswald as an expert adviser. Nevertheless they take the position they are entitled to cross-examine each other's witnesses on the basis that while there may be common issues in their defence, there are adverse interests between them on the pleadings and on the issues before this Court. The fact that there are no pleadings between them and no issue of contribution or indemnity to be adjudicated upon on the record in the action does not, in their submission, result in the conclusion that there is no adversity of interests between them. It is clear from the pleadings, the issues and the evidence in this case that Hardy and Western Caissons have interests that are adverse between them. For example, to successfully defend each must show it was not negligent in any way that contributed to the alleged negligent loss of ground control. One way to do that is to show there was negligence on the part of the co-Defendants that was the sole cause of the alleged excessive ground movement that caused the damages. Therefore, should Hardy and Western Caissons be permitted to examine each other's witnesses? The law in this area is far from precise. In Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant The Law of Evidence in Canada, the learned authors address these points at p. 862 thusly: In cases where there are co-defendants with similar interests who have pleaded separately and are represented by different counsel, a trial judge has a discretion to refuse to allow counsel for one defendant to cross-examine a co-defendant's witnesses. If, however, the interests of the parties are not similar, separate counsel are usually allowed to cross-examine a co-defendant or that co-defendant's witnesses. The authority quoted for this statement is Millar v. British Columbia Rapid Transit Co., [1926] 1 W.W.R. 543 (B.C. C.A.). In that case, Macdonald, C.J.A. in the majority judgment referred to several English authorities, particularly Lord v. Colvin (1855), 24 L.J. Ch. 517, 61 E.R. 888. He cited from Lord v. Colvin, only the conclusions of the Judges as stated by Kindersley, V.C.: The opinion then of the whole of the judges is, that a defendant may cross-examine a co-defendant's witnesses. When the evidence is taken, whether by examination in chief or on cross-examination, the whole is common to all parties. However, Macdonald, C.J.A. deduced from his examination of Lord v. Colvin and the authorities cited therein the following rule: The rule, I think, to be deduced from the authorities is, that in respect of trials in civil actions (leaving aside divorce) separate counsel should not be heard in cases in which the parties have not pleaded separately; that when they have pleaded separately but there is no substantial difference in their interests, the Judge may refuse to allow separate representation or cross-examination of co-defendant's witnesses, and that in other circumstances separate counsel may be allowed to be heard with the consequential right to cross-examine a co-defendant or his witnesses. … These cases review the English authorities and grapple with the differences in the English Rules which refer to the “opposite party” as opposed to the Canadian Rules based on “parties adverse in interest”. Without entering into that debate what is certain from these authorities is that in civil actions (1) as between defendants there is a right to examine in chief a co-defendant's witness by way of supplementary questions; (2) there is a right to cross-examine a co-defendant's witness on points where the other defendant is a party adverse in interest or, where a co-defendant's witness has by his or her evidence adversely affected the other defendant's position in the case. Adverse in interest is to be interpreted broadly to include rights to be adjudicated upon or a pecuniary or other substantial legal interest or conflict in the action. In the Rose & Laflamme case [[1923] 2 W.W.R. 1067 at 1069ff. (Sask. C.A.)] Lamont, J.A. defined adverse in interest as follows: To my mind, ‘a party adverse in interest’ is not necessarily limited to a party with whom an issue is to be adjudicated upon by the Court in action. There are cases … where, although no issue is stated between certain defendants, their interests are as adverse as if they were upon opposite sides of the record. In my opinion, therefore, under our Rules a party to a cause or matter may be said to be adverse in interest to another if he has a direct pecuniary or other substantial legal interest adverse to the legal interest of the other party, even although they may be upon the same side of the record and there is no issue on the record that the court will be called upon to adjudicate between them. See also Menzies v. McLeod[(1915), 25 D.L.R. 777 at 779ff. (Ont. H.C.)]… where Boyd C. stated: An actual issue in tangible form spread upon the record is not essential, so long as there is a manifest adverse interest in one defendant as against another defendant. ‘Adverse interest’ is a flexible term, meaning pecuniary interest, or any other substantial interest in the subject-matter of litigation. Finally in The Conduct of an Action, Williston, Q.C. and Rolls, Q.C., at p. 100, after quoting the above two citations go on to state: He [referring to Boyd C. in Menzies v. McLeod] also observed that if an issue existed between the co-defendants, they may be adverse in interest even though both are resisting the plaintiff's claim. Thus a defendant may cross-examine a co-defendant or any other witness who has given evidence against him. In every instance, the underlying requirement for the right to cross-examine is the conflicting nature or hostile effect of the evidence on the party who claims the right of cross-examination. In Frobisher Ltd. v. Canadian Pipelines & Petroleums Ltd. et al.; Daigle and Mackinnon v. Canadian Pipelines & Petroleums Ltd. (1957), 10 D.L.R. (2d) 338, the trial judge refused to allow the defendant company the opportunity to cross-examine two co-defendants in the main action, who were also plaintiffs by counterclaim against the defendant company, except insofar as the cross-examination might relate to the counterclaim. It was held on appeal by the majority that the trial judge was wrong in his ruling because, while all defendants were in common interest with each other under their pleadings to the statement of claim, nonetheless the two co-defendants had given evidence adverse to the defendant company and hence the cross-examination should have been allowed. An appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was dismissed; Locke J. and Martland J. expressly agreed with the view of the majority of the Court of Appeal that permission to cross-examine should not have been refused. (my emphasis) Based on these authorities, I have decided, first, that the Defendants may examine the witnesses of other co-Defendants by way of examination-in-chief, to elicit supplementary evidence in support of their position on matters common between them. Second, that the Defendants may cross-examine witnesses of a co-Defendant where either upon the record or on the issues raised in the case, there are adversities of interest or rights to be adjudicated or conflicts on the evidence between them. The subject area of this cross-examination should be conducted only with the prior approval of the Court to guard against procedural or substantive abuses. Third, that having regard to the circumstances of this case, the examination by one Defendant of a co-Defendant should proceed prior to the cross-examination by the Plaintiff Trizec. Fourth, that following cross-examination by Trizec of a Defendant's witness, a co-Defendant may apply to deal with a matter by way of further cross-examination in the event that the Plaintiff's cross-examination has raised a new adverse point in issue. 5. Entering documents as evidence on motions In Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp., 2002 ABQB 403, 2002 CarswellAlta 547, 316 A.R. 1, 7 Alta. L.R. (4th) 369, one of the parties on a motion sought to refer to a document which had been listed in an affidavit of records filed by one of the parties. McMahon J. did not allow the document to be put into evidence in that manner. At pp. 8-9, his Lordship said: In my view … a document is not admissible on an application merely because it has been listed on an affidavit of records. An affidavit of records serves a different purpose than an affidavit for an application, which narrows the issues and evidence, gives the opposing party an idea of the case it faces, and allows the opposing party a chance to cross-examine on the affidavit and any attached materials. The affidavits of records in these proceedings contain hundreds, if not thousands, of documents. To admit any or all of those on an application without more would be unfair. In general, for a document to be admissible on an application, it will be exhibited to an affidavit, identified during cross-examination on an affidavit or during examination for discovery, or introduced through a witness. It may also be admissible by consent, by statutory authority … or by a notice to admit (rule 230). In Ellis-Don Management Services v. Rae-Dawn Construction Ltd. (1992), 131 A.R. 190, the Alberta Court of Appeal considered an appeal from an order which directed that the evidence from one action apply in another action where there were different parties. The actions all related to the same construction failure but some involved insurance claims and some involved actions on unpaid accounts. Use of affidavit evidence 1.
Generally Rule 261(1) provides that normally facts are proven at trial through viva voce evidence.
Rule 261(2) gives the trial judge discretion to permit a fact to be proven by affidavit or to permit an affidavit to be read in.
This must be done either before or during the trial itself.
The rule then limits this discretion by providing that such orders shall not be made where the other party bona fide desires to cross-examine a witness who could be produced.

In other jurisdictions similar rules have been interpreted in such a manner to indicate that the proper practice is to bring an application for leave to read an affidavit as evidence before the trial: Rae v.
446 (Sask.
C.A.); Rzani v.
Rzani, [1950] 2 W.W.R.
73 (Sask.
However, in both of these uncontested divorce cases exceptions were made and the affidavits were considered because of special circumstances.
I can find no special circumstances in this case for reading from the affidavit because the absence of the affiant was not satisfactorily explained.
I am also satisfied that the solicitor for the applicant would have a bona fide desire to cross-examine any other of the affiants who were not called as witnesses.
In Ontario, proof of any fact at trial by means of affidavit without a motion for an order by the judge is considered irregular: Parker v.
Parker, [1948] O.W.N.
834 (H.C.); Thorne v.
Thorne, [1951] O.W.N.
Rule 261(3) has also been considered.

It provides that if the matter has commenced by originating notice of motion upon any application or motion evidence may be given by affidavit unless these rules otherwise provide or the court otherwise directs.
However, the use which can be made of an affidavit once it is filed is specified in R.
13, which limits the use of affidavits to applications in chambers.
Since this was a trial and not a chambers application, this rule does not apply.

I therefore exclude any evidence contained in the affidavits because no proper application was brought before the court to adduce affidavit evidence and the solicitor for the applicant would be denied the right to cross-examination at the trial on the material contained in the affidavit.
Coronado Developments Ltd. v.
W.E.D.
Developments Ltd.
L.R.
(2d) 34 (Q.B.), at 40-41, per Cawsey J.
In United Inc. v.
Canadian National Railway Company, 2021 ABQB 356, 2021 CarswellAlta 1102, the affiant of an affidavit died before he was cross-examined on his affidavit.
The issue before Justice Rothwell was whether the affidavit could be admitted into evidence in the trial pursuant to Rule 8.17.

Justice Rothwell said: [17] Both parties agree that the Hussey Affidavit is hearsay but that it can potentially be admitted if it meets the principled exception approach to hearsay, in other words, if the Affidavit is necessary and reliable: Canmore Mountain Villas Inc v Alberta (Minister of Seniors and Comunity Supports), 2010 ABQB 489 (Canmore).
[18]Canmore dealt with an application to admit the affidavit evidence of Mr.
Craig, a former mayor of Canmore, who had sworn an affidavit and later died.
Unlike the present case, Mr.
Craig had been examined on his affidavit prior to his death.
[19]Canmore considered Rule 261 of the Alberta Rules of Court.
Rule 8.17 is the successor to Rule 261.

In Canmore, at para 26, Justice Veit held: Although the most recent principled exceptions to the hearsay rule were developed by the Supreme Court of Canada in the context of criminal law, a fortiori—that is, with even greater force—the principles apply in civil proceedings where, of course, the onus of proof is lower than in criminal proceedings.
Indeed, the application of the principle has been accepted in numerous civil proceedings, including by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal: Eric Whebby Ltd.

In that context, I note that the comments in Pierre relating to the criminal context in which the contemporary Canadian standard of admissibility of hearsay evidence was developed was merely intended to show that the Khan, Smith, Khelawon, etc. line of cases was merely intended to enlarge the scope of admissible hearsay, not to narrow it.

[20] Justice Graesser also considered Rule 261, and followed a similar analysis, in Brennenstuhl Estate v Trynchy, 2007 ABQB 647 (Brennenstuhl Estate). … [23] In Brennenstuhl Estate Justice Graesser stated at paragraph 36: … Necessity does not require that the proponent establish that there is no other way of getting similar evidence before the court.
Rather, it relates to the ability to get this particular evidence before the court.
If the proposed evidence is relevant, then necessity suggests that such evidence should be before the court in its search for truth.
Necessity in relation to hearsay evidence is to be considered in the context of determining whether the evidence from this witness can be obtained and admitted in some other way.

Where the witness has died without being examined de bene esse, for example, resort to prior statements or testimony is clearly necessary, as that witness's evidence cannot be obtained in any other way.
The fact that there is some other witness who may give similar evidence is not an answer to necessity.

(Emphasis in original) [24] Justice Veit, in Canmore at para 29, relying on the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in R v B(KG), 1993 CanLII 116 (SCC), [1993] 1 SCR 740 noted that the death of a witness will, in most situations, be sufficient to meet the necessity criteria. … Reliability [28] Again both parties agree that at this stage a Court should focus on “threshold reliability” as opposed to “ultimate reliability”.
Ultimate reliability will be determined at the conclusion of the trial.
[29] United provided the following list of reliability factors:
(a) Existence of an oath
(b) The nature of the affiant
(c) How long after the fact was the affidavit sworn
(d) The nature of the evidence
(e) The context in which the affidavit was sworn
(f) The importance of the evidence
(g) Whether the affiant had a motive to lie
(h) Whether the evidence is corroborated or appears to have a solid foundation
(i) Whether the evidence is internally inconsistent, or conflicts with other evidence; and
(j) Whether there was an opportunity to cross-examine the affiant, and if so, whether there is a reasonable explanation for failing to do so.
[30] These factors are drawn from Jans v Jans, 2015 SKQB 226 at para 25 (Jans).

While Jans is a Saskatchewan case I accept that the above factors, while not comprehensive, are relevant considerations. … Prejudice [39] In Brennenstuhl Estate Justice Graesser relied upon the Canned Heat Marketing Inc v CFM International Inc, [1998] BCJ No.
1722 (SC) decision and held that the party opposing the affidavit's introduction bears the onus of establishing prejudice: para 24.

[40] Justice Graesser adopted Master Bolton's approach, described at para 25: Master Bolton noted that the fact that disputed evidence would be admitted at trial contrary to the interests of the party opposed was not enough to establish prejudice.
Instead, there must be a weighing of prejudice, because presumably the party seeking to admit the evidence will always be prejudiced if it was not allowed to present its evidence.
The court is left to weigh the prejudice to each side.

[41] I adopt Justice Graesser's approach. … [48] While the Hussey Affidavit can be admitted under the principled exception to the hearsay rule it still must be reviewed for compliance with the rules of evidence: Canmore at para 47.
United correctly points out that evidence that would not be permitted in viva voce testimony should not be permitted by way of affidavit. … 2.

Purpose of Rule … although this Rule does not specifically say so, it is my view that the Rule was intended to allow—in certain instances—a witness to give evidence in a proceeding by way of affidavit as opposed to having to appear personally and give evidence viva voce.
It is not to permit an affidavit in a different matter altogether to be simply read in as proof of the contents.

Montreal Trust Co.
L.R.
357, per Hawco J.
Timing of Application … the proper practice is to apply for leave under Rule 261(2) before the trial as opposed to at the trial.
Heritage Freehold Specialists & Co. v.
Montreal Trust Co.
L.R.
357 (Q.B.), per Hawco J.

Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd.
L.R.

At trial, the plaintiff objected to one defendant being allowed to cross-examine witnesses called by another defendant on the ground that the defendants had cooperated in the defence of the matter.
In ruling on the right to cross-examine, Mason J. said, at pp.
445-48: Counsel for Trizec are concerned because of the manifest co-operation between these Defendants in defending the action.
Trizec's counsel submit that in the proceedings before this Court there has been obvious co-operation between these two Defendants.
For instance, they argue that Mr.

Oswald, an expert in geotechnical engineering, has been advising both Counsel for Western Caissons and Hardy with respect to geotechnical matters during trial particularly during the conduct of both Counsel's cross-examination of several of the Trizec witnesses.
Counsel for Western Caissons and Hardy are alive to these concerns and acknowledge their consultations with Mr.
Oswald as an expert adviser.

Nevertheless they take the position they are entitled to cross-examine each other's witnesses on the basis that while there may be common issues in their defence, there are adverse interests between them on the pleadings and on the issues before this Court.

The fact that there are no pleadings between them and no issue of contribution or indemnity to be adjudicated upon on the record in the action does not, in their submission, result in the conclusion that there is no adversity of interests between them.
It is clear from the pleadings, the issues and the evidence in this case that Hardy and Western Caissons have interests that are adverse between them.
For example, to successfully defend each must show it was not negligent in any way that contributed to the alleged negligent loss of ground control.
One way to do that is to show there was negligence on the part of the co-Defendants that was the sole cause of the alleged excessive ground movement that caused the damages.
Therefore, should Hardy and Western Caissons be permitted to examine each other's witnesses?
The law in this area is far from precise.
In Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant The Law of Evidence in Canada, the learned authors address these points at p.

862 thusly: In cases where there are co-defendants with similar interests who have pleaded separately and are represented by different counsel, a trial judge has a discretion to refuse to allow counsel for one defendant to cross-examine a co-defendant's witnesses.
If, however, the interests of the parties are not similar, separate counsel are usually allowed to cross-examine a co-defendant or that co-defendant's witnesses.
The authority quoted for this statement is Millar v.
British Columbia Rapid Transit Co., [1926] 1 W.W.R.
In that case, Macdonald, C.J.A. in the majority judgment referred to several English authorities, particularly Lord v.
Colvin (1855), 24 L.J.
Ch.
He cited from Lord v.
Colvin, only the conclusions of the Judges as stated by Kindersley, V.C.: The opinion then of the whole of the judges is, that a defendant may cross-examine a co-defendant's witnesses.
When the evidence is taken, whether by examination in chief or on cross-examination, the whole is common to all parties.
However, Macdonald, C.J.A. deduced from his examination of Lord v.

Colvin and the authorities cited therein the following rule: The rule, I think, to be deduced from the authorities is, that in respect of trials in civil actions (leaving aside divorce) separate counsel should not be heard in cases in which the parties have not pleaded separately; that when they have pleaded separately but there is no substantial difference in their interests, the Judge may refuse to allow separate representation or cross-examination of co-defendant's witnesses, and that in other circumstances separate counsel may be allowed to be heard with the consequential right to cross-examine a co-defendant or his witnesses. … These cases review the English authorities and grapple with the differences in the English Rules which refer to the “opposite party” as opposed to the Canadian Rules based on “parties adverse in interest”.

(1) as between defendants there is a right to examine in chief a co-defendant's witness by way of supplementary questions

(2) there is a right to cross-examine a co-defendant's witness on points where the other defendant is a party adverse in interest or, where a co-defendant's witness has by his or her evidence adversely affected the other defendant's position in the case.
Adverse in interest is to be interpreted broadly to include rights to be adjudicated upon or a pecuniary or other substantial legal interest or conflict in the action.
In the Rose & Laflamme case [[1923] 2 W.W.R.
(Sask.

C.A.)] Lamont, J.A. defined adverse in interest as follows: To my mind, ‘a party adverse in interest’ is not necessarily limited to a party with whom an issue is to be adjudicated upon by the Court in action.
There are cases … where, although no issue is stated between certain defendants, their interests are as adverse as if they were upon opposite sides of the record.

In my opinion, therefore, under our Rules a party to a cause or matter may be said to be adverse in interest to another if he has a direct pecuniary or other substantial legal interest adverse to the legal interest of the other party, even although they may be upon the same side of the record and there is no issue on the record that the court will be called upon to adjudicate between them.
See also Menzies v.
McLeod[(1915), 25 D.L.R.
(Ont.

H.C.)]… where Boyd C. stated: An actual issue in tangible form spread upon the record is not essential, so long as there is a manifest adverse interest in one defendant as against another defendant. ‘Adverse interest’ is a flexible term, meaning pecuniary interest, or any other substantial interest in the subject-matter of litigation.
Finally in The Conduct of an Action, Williston, Q.C. and Rolls, Q.C., at p.
100, after quoting the above two citations go on to state: He [referring to Boyd C. in Menzies v.
McLeod] also observed that if an issue existed between the co-defendants, they may be adverse in interest even though both are resisting the plaintiff's claim.
Thus a defendant may cross-examine a co-defendant or any other witness who has given evidence against him.
In every instance, the underlying requirement for the right to cross-examine is the conflicting nature or hostile effect of the evidence on the party who claims the right of cross-examination.
In Frobisher Ltd. v.
Canadian Pipelines & Petroleums Ltd. et al.; Daigle and Mackinnon v.
Canadian Pipelines & Petroleums Ltd.

It was held on appeal by the majority that the trial judge was wrong in his ruling because, while all defendants were in common interest with each other under their pleadings to the statement of claim, nonetheless the two co-defendants had given evidence adverse to the defendant company and hence the cross-examination should have been allowed.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.20:1 Rule 8.20 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.20. Motion for dismissal 1. Test In Horizon Resource Management Ltd. v. Blaze Energy Ltd., 2013 ABCA 139, 2013 CarswellAlta 446, 544 A.R. 289, 78 Alta. L.R. (5th) 353, the Court said, at paragraph 25: 25 A ruling on a nonsuit is reviewed for correctness: Capital Estate Planning Corporation v. Lynch, 2011 ABCA 224 at para 19, 510 AR 244, quoting from Prudential Securities Credit Corp, LLc v. Cobrand Foods Ltd, 2007 ONCA 425, 85 OR (3d) 561 at para 35: On a non-suit motion, the trial judge undertakes a limited inquiry. Two relevant principles that guide this enquiry are these. First, if a plaintiff puts forward some evidence on all elements of its claim, the judge must dismiss the motion. Second, in assessing whether a plaintiff has made out a prima facie case, the judge must assume the evidence to be true and must assign “the most favourable meaning” to evidence capable of giving rise to competing inferences. In Harvey v. Black (1993), 7 Alta. L.R. (3d) 103 (Q.B.) at p. 109, the Court said: If, on a central issue, the plaintiff fails to present at least some evidence on which the trier of fact could base a finding in its favour, no case has been made out, and the defendant is entitled to its nonsuit. The test was summarized in Foley v. Alberta (Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act), 2002 ABCA 297, 2002 CarswellAlta 1623, 330 A.R. 1, 15 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231. Fruman J.A. (with O'Leary J.A. concurring on this point), said, at p. 11: The Mallets argue that the trial judge improperly dismissed their application for a non-suit motion at the close of the Administrator's case. They do not challenge the test used by the trial judge. The judge stated at AB 199/39-45 (quoting from John Sopinka & Sidney N. Lederman, The Law of Evidence in Civil Cases (Toronto: Butterworths, 1974) at p. 521) that a judge: […] must conclude whether a reasonable jury could find in the plaintiff's favour if it believed the evidence given in trial up to that point. The judge does not decide whether the jury will accept the evidence, but whether the inference that the plaintiff seeks in his favour could be drawn from the evidence adduced, if the jury chose to accept it. The judge did not err in her formulation of the test, which is consistent with other authorities. See Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877), 3 App. Cas. 193 at p. 207 (H.L.); Gwyllt, Re, [1944] 2 D.L.R. 512 at p. 515 (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Mezzo, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 802, 68 N.R. 1, 43 Man. R. (2d) 161 at p. 837 [S.C.R.]; Harvey and Peterson v. Black (1992), 137 A.R. 111 at p. 116 (Q.B.). paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.21:1 Rule 8.21 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.21. When May a Court Refuse Jury's Verdict In Palpal-Latoc v. Berstad, 2003 ABQB 236, 2003 CarswellAlta 367, 337 A.R. 102, 15 Alta. L.R. (4th) 187, the Plaintiff asked the court to set aside the jury's damage award and substitute the Court's assessment on the grounds that “the verdict given by the jury assessing damages in this case was so plainly unreasonable and unjust that it could not have been reached by them reviewing and understanding the evidence as a whole and acting judicially.” In dismissing the application, Brooker J. discussed the limited circumstances in which a jury's verdict can be set aside by the Court. At pp. 108-109, his Lordship said: Whereas the Alberta Rules of Court appear to give the Court of Appeal a wide jurisdiction to deal with jury verdicts on appeal [Rule 505], the Rules only give a trial judge a limited jurisdiction to deal with jury verdicts [Rules 257, 258, and 259]. None of these rules contemplate or authorize the trial judge to substitute his or her verdict for that of the jury. Rather, the relief generally authorized is that of a retrial. In the result, on the basis of the common law as well as our Rules of Court, I conclude that a judge in Alberta has a limited jurisdiction to refuse to enter or otherwise deal with a jury's damages assessment. I further conclude that a trial judge cannot simply set aside the damage assessment of the jury and substitute his or her own assessment of damages. (ii) What is the test to be applied? The test generally used by a court of appeal in setting aside a jury verdict on damages has been discussed in a number of cases [see footnote 5]. The most precise and encompassing version of the test is found in the Court of Appeal decision in Vaillancourt[Vaillancourt v. Molnar Estate (2002), 176 B.C.A.C. 109]. In that decision, at paragraph 27, the Court quotes from Bisson v. Powell River (District) (1967), 62 W.W.R. (N.S.) 707, (B.C. C.A.), at p. 721: I now consider whether, apart from any misdirection or non-direction, the jury's award was so excessive as to be wholly ‘out of proportion’ and plainly so unreasonable that no jury acting judicially could have reached it. I refer to the test for a court of appeal because wording similar to this was used by the Plaintiff in his Notion of Motion upon which this application is based. … However, I am satisfied that the test to be applied by a trial judge is not the same as that applicable to the court of appeal. In Olszynko v. Larocque et al., [1998] O.J. No. 5281, 83 O.T.C. 49 (Gen. Div.); affd. (1999) 127 O.A.C. 162 (C.A.); leave to appeal to SCC denied [1999] S.C.C.A. No. 607, 259 N.R. 398, 139 O.A.C. 400), Sedgwick, J., at paragraph 20, quotes Carruthers, J., in Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto and Manning (1992), 7 O.R. (3d) 489 (Gen. Div.): That statement has been taken to mean that a trial judge may refuse to accept the verdict of a jury only when she or he considers that there is no evidence to support the findings of the jury, or where the jury gives an answer to a question which cannot in law provide a foundation for a judgment. … . . . . . Having regard to the foregoing, I conclude that the proper test is that a trial judge may only refuse to accept a jury's verdict when there is no evidence to support the verdict or where the verdict is contrary to law or in the limited and special circumstances set out in the Rules of Court earlier quoted. Further, I conclude that in those rare circumstances where the trial judge is entitled to refuse to accept a jury's verdict, the trial judge's options are limited. If the jury verdict is contrary to law, as for example in ter Neuzen[Neuzen v. Korn, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 674 (S.C.C.)] where nonpecuniary damages greatly exceeded the “cap”, the trial judge is not entitled to substitute his or her own assessment of the damages. Rather, the trial judge is only entitled to reduce the award to conform with the legal maximum or cap. In those circumstances where the issue is whether or not there is any evidence, the trial judge is not entitled to weigh the evidence. The duty of the trial judge is to determine whether or not there is any evidence to support the verdict. If there is some evidence, the trial judge should enter judgment accordingly. If there is no evidence to support the verdict, the trial judge should not enter that verdict. The situations set out in the Rules of Court generally mandate a retrial in the circumstances described there. In no event, in my opinion, is the trial judge entitled to set aside a jury's assessment of damages and make the assessment of the damages he or she thinks should be awarded. The law as stated in Palpal-Latoc v. Berstad was approved and applied in Goulbourne v. Buoy, 2004 ABQB 70, 2003 CarswellAlta 1918, 350 A.R. 245; additional reasons at 2003 ABQB 1029, 2003 CarswellAlta 1775, 350 A.R. 256, by Read J.

In the result, on the basis of the common law as well as our Rules of Court, I conclude that a judge in Alberta has a limited jurisdiction to refuse to enter or otherwise deal with a jury's damages assessment.
I further conclude that a trial judge cannot simply set aside the damage assessment of the jury and substitute his or her own assessment of damages.
(ii) What is the test to be applied?
The test generally used by a court of appeal in setting aside a jury verdict on damages has been discussed in a number of cases [see footnote 5].
The most precise and encompassing version of the test is found in the Court of Appeal decision in Vaillancourt[Vaillancourt v.
Molnar Estate (2002), 176 B.C.A.C.
In that decision, at paragraph 27, the Court quotes from Bisson v.
Powell River (District) (1967), 62 W.W.R.
C.A.), at p.

721: I now consider whether, apart from any misdirection or non-direction, the jury's award was so excessive as to be wholly ‘out of proportion’ and plainly so unreasonable that no jury acting judicially could have reached it.

I refer to the test for a court of appeal because wording similar to this was used by the Plaintiff in his Notion of Motion upon which this application is based. … However, I am satisfied that the test to be applied by a trial judge is not the same as that applicable to the court of appeal.
In Olszynko v.
Larocque et al., [1998] O.J.
No.
49 (Gen.
Div.); affd.
162 (C.A.); leave to appeal to SCC denied [1999] S.C.C.A.
No.
400), Sedgwick, J., at paragraph 20, quotes Carruthers, J., in Hill v.
Church of Scientology of Toronto and Manning (1992), 7 O.R.

Div.): That statement has been taken to mean that a trial judge may refuse to accept the verdict of a jury only when she or he considers that there is no evidence to support the findings of the jury, or where the jury gives an answer to a question which cannot in law provide a foundation for a judgment. … . . . . .

Having regard to the foregoing, I conclude that the proper test is that a trial judge may only refuse to accept a jury's verdict when there is no evidence to support the verdict or where the verdict is contrary to law or in the limited and special circumstances set out in the Rules of Court earlier quoted.
Further, I conclude that in those rare circumstances where the trial judge is entitled to refuse to accept a jury's verdict, the trial judge's options are limited.
If the jury verdict is contrary to law, as for example in ter Neuzen[Neuzen v.
674 (S.C.C.)] where nonpecuniary damages greatly exceeded the “cap”, the trial judge is not entitled to substitute his or her own assessment of the damages.
Rather, the trial judge is only entitled to reduce the award to conform with the legal maximum or cap.
In those circumstances where the issue is whether or not there is any evidence, the trial judge is not entitled to weigh the evidence.
The duty of the trial judge is to determine whether or not there is any evidence to support the verdict.
If there is some evidence, the trial judge should enter judgment accordingly.
If there is no evidence to support the verdict, the trial judge should not enter that verdict.
The situations set out in the Rules of Court generally mandate a retrial in the circumstances described there.
In no event, in my opinion, is the trial judge entitled to set aside a jury's assessment of damages and make the assessment of the damages he or she thinks should be awarded.
The law as stated in Palpal-Latoc v.
Berstad was approved and applied in Goulbourne v.
Buoy, 2004 ABQB 70, 2003 CarswellAlta 1918, 350 A.R.
245; additional reasons at 2003 ABQB 1029, 2003 CarswellAlta 1775, 350 A.R.
256, by Read J.

sentences.text: Accidents and mistakes

paragraphs.text: (1) If by an accident, mistake or other cause a party does not prove a fact or record important to the party's case, the Court may (a) proceed with the trial subject to the fact or record being proved as ordered by the Court, or (b) if the action is being tried by a jury, make an order under subrule (2). (2) The Court may (a) adjourn the jury sittings, or (b) if the fact or record is one the formal proof of which could not seriously be challenged, (i) the Court may direct the jury to find a verdict as if the fact or record had been proved, and (ii) the jury's verdict then takes effect when the fact or record is proved before the Court. (3) If a fact or record is not proved as referred to in subrule (2)(b)(ii), judgment must be entered for the opposite party unless the Court otherwise orders. (4) The Court may make a costs award with respect to any issue arising out of or as a result of the operation of this rule.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.24:1 Rule 8.24 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.24. 1. Use of Rule In Ward v. Knowles (1982), 34 A.R. 286 (Q.B.), at 298-300, Kirby J. dealt with a situation in which counsel wished to produce further evidence concerning the effect of inflation on the plaintiff's loss of earnings. The reason advanced for tendering this evidence was a decision handed down in this court on April 16, 1981 but not reported until September 1 after the plaintiff's case had been closed. The case Henrikson v. Parke et al. is reported in (1981), 29 A.R. 431. It was held in that case that the plaintiff who had been awarded damages for loss of earnings to date of trial was entitled to have his loss of income from the date of the accident in 1977 to the date of trial calculated on the basis of the 1981 hourly rate, … to adjust the award for depreciation of the dollar resulting from inflation … It is argued that the Rule is not applicable in a situation of this kind. In my view it is. In Kowalenko v. Lewis and Lepine, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 504 (S.C.S.) … Turgeon, J.A., for the court at p. 507 observed with respect to Rule 354 of the Saskatchewan Rules of Court which is identical in wording to Alberta Rule 249(a): This Rule is not to be found among the English Rules, and I believe that is should be used sparingly and only where a clearly meritorious case is made out and where a substantial injustice might otherwise be done, as no doubt it is a rule easily susceptible of abuse and liable, if too freely applied, to serve as an encouragement to carelessness. Since the decision in the Hendrickson case did not come to the attention of counsel for the plaintiff until it was reported after the plaintiff's case had been closed, and since to exclude an adjustment in the claim for damages for loss of income to date of trial so as to allow for depreciation in the value of the dollar due to inflation would in my view do a substantial injustice to the plaintiff, I considered it appropriate to admit the statement of adjustment. 2. Test to Be Applied Then it is argued that the evidence ought not to be admitted in the particular circumstances of this case. It is said that the defendant's counsel having considered the whole case prior to and during the trial and having decided not to give his own evidence in the belief that the other evidence at his command was sufficient for his purposes and having closed his case on that basis, he ought not to be allowed now to give the evidence which he deliberately withheld. The answer of defendant's counsel is that the evidence which he then had was deficient as to dates and would not therefore have much effect. He says that he has since the hearing discovered the lacking dates and is now desirous of giving the evidence. I do not think it necessary here to refer to decisions of the Appellate Division on applications to that Court to receive fresh evidence. The rule governing the right of a trial Judge to hear further evidence, after the close of the trial and before judgment, would appear to be less stringent. In Stevenson v. Dandy, [1918] 3 W.W.R. 662 … Beck, J., in the course of a lengthy judgment, said: He [the trial Judge] is the one in the best position to judge of its bearing upon the case in the light of the evidence already given. In considering such material I think a Judge dealing with such an application is not bound by the same rule as is a Court of Appeal on an application to hear further evidence or to grant a new trial for the purpose of the further evidence being given … It should be said, however, in this case the Chief Justice with whom Stuart and Hyndman, JJ. concurred, merely agreed with Beck, J. in holding that the trial Judge was in error in thinking that he had no jurisdiction to hear new evidence. In Calder v. Int. Harvester Co., [1918] 2 W.W.R. 905, 11 Sask. L.R. 244, Taylor, J. said that while in the exercise of his discretion a trial Judge may, until judgment has been delivered, re-open the trial, he should do so with the greatest care and he should not permit a party after learning that the finding of the Court is adverse, to seek to supplement his proof by the production of documents which he should, and knew he should, have at the trial. This seems to be as far as it goes a salutary rule. Brett v. Brett, [1937] 2 W.W.R. 689 (Alta. T.D.), at 691-92, per Ewing J. Brett was appealed and the Court of Appeal said: The plaintiff appeals from the order allowing the evidence to be given ([1937] 2 W.W.R. 689) but it was clearly a matter for the discretion of the trial Judge, and he quite properly considered that the matter of first importance was the rights of the litigants which should not be jeopardized by any oversight or mistake on the part of solicitor or counsel. Certainly the trial Judge should, and no doubt did, examine the evidence with much care, but the weight to be given to it was entirely for his consideration and if he thought proper to accept it as truthful, as he did, we would not be justified in differing from him. Brett v. Brett, [1938] 2 W.W.R. 368 at 372 (Alta. C.A.).

paragraphs.text: 8.25. Use of streamlined trial
paragraphs.heading: Part 8. Trial

sentences.text: Use of streamlined trial

paragraphs.text: (1) The Court, on application by a party or on the Court's own motion, may order or direct that a court action be resolved by a streamlined trial if the Court is satisfied that (a) it is necessary for the purpose of the action to be fairly and justly resolved, and (b) it is proportionate to the importance and complexity of the issues, the amounts involved and the resources that can reasonably be allocated to resolving the dispute. (2) An order or direction under subrule (1) may be made at any time, including in chambers, at a case conference meeting or case management meeting, at an application for judgment or at any other appearance. (3) A streamlined trial shall not be considered as a disproportionate process solely because (a) issues of credibility may arise, (b) some oral evidence may be required at the trial, (c) cross-examination of some witnesses may be required, or (d) expert evidence may be introduced. Alta. Reg. 126/2023, s. 11

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 8.25:1 Rule 8.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 8.25. 1. Overview In Bailey v. Northern Alberta Institute of Technology, 2024 ABKB 563, Justice Mah discussed the rules governing streamlined trials: [3] A two-part test governs the exercise of judicial discretion in granting or denying a streamlined trial: • First, a streamlined trial is necessary for the purpose of the action to be fairly and justly resolved; and • Second, the streamlined trial must be proportionate to the importance and complexity of the issues, the amounts involved and the resources that can reasonably be allocated to resolving the dispute, See: Rule 8.25(1); Arsenault v Big Rock Brewery, 2024 ABKB 387 at para 16; Hou v Canadian North Inc, 2024 ABKB 549 at paras 11-17. [4] The party that applies for a streamlined trial bears the onus of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the streamlined trial is both necessary and proportionate. …. [6] Current Rule 8.25(3) itself provides that the presence of credibility issues, and that some oral evidence and some cross-examination might be required are not bars to a streamlined trial. Further, the Notice to the Profession and Public (NPP) #2023-02, which announced the arrival of the streamlined trial process in Alberta, gives “wrongful dismissal actions” as one example of matters that will often be suitable for a streamlined trial. [7] Those submissions by Mr. Bailey’s counsel are all correct, but not determinative. The actual criteria of “necessity” for the purpose of the action and “proportionality” must be established to the required standard. It is not inevitable that wrongful dismissal actions are dealt with by of streamlined trial. [8] Armstrong J at para 22 of Arsenault listed in non-exhaustive fashion some of the characteristics of necessity: … 1. Where the streamlined trial will create a more efficient process by eliminating unnecessary steps and reducing overall delay in the resolution of the dispute. 2. Where the streamlined trial will result in a more cost-effective process for the parties. 3. Where the streamlined trial will enhance the administration of justice by making more efficient use of court resources and provide litigants with a more accessible and timely dispute resolution process. 4. Where the streamlined trial will result in a more sharply focused process and the elimination of complexities in the form of interim applications that do not bear on the ultimate resolution of the real issues in dispute. 5. Where it would be unjust to require the parties to proceed to a full trial, considering the value and complexity of the dispute. 6. Where the streamlined trial process will simplify the proceeding to make it easier for the parties to assess the strengths and weaknesses of their positions and thereby potentially reach a resolution without the need for a trial. [9] In Hou, Renke J added this gloss at paras 21 & 22: [21] The necessity standard requires the moving party to show more than that it would be possible for a streamlined trial to achieve a fair and just result or that a streamlined trial would have the potential to achieve the fair and just result. It is true, as NPP#2023-02 states, that streamlined trial “is used when an Action can be fairly and justly resolved” by that process (emphasis added), in the sense that if an action could not be fairly and justly resolved by that process the streamlined trial application could not succeed. But the application should not succeed if the moving party shows only that a streamlined trial is one way of achieving a fair and just result. The term “necessity” imports exclusivity, the identification of the single means of achieving the fair and just result. [22] Necessity, I observe, could be established by showing that an action can be fairly and justly resolved by streamlined trial but not by the ordinary trial process. Exclusivity can be established by eliminating alternatives. [10] On the topic of proportionality, Arsenault at para 39 applies some of the relevant criteria related to summary trials, stating: At this stage of the analysis, some of the jurisprudence relating to summary trials can be instructive. When considering whether a streamlined trial is a proportionate process, many of the factors that were considered in relation to the suitability of a summary trial are applicable. These factors include the amount involved, the complexity of the matter, the urgency, any prejudice likely to arise by reason of delay, the cost of a trial, the course of the proceedings, the need to cross examine witnesses in court, the necessity of questioning for discovery and whether resolution of the matter will depend on findings of credibility: Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v Crossroads C&I Distributors, 2013 ABQB 702 at para 23; Duff v Oshust, 2005 ABQB 117 at para. 24. [11] While it might be said that the twin elements of necessity and proportionality in Rule 8.25(1) overlap, as Renke J points out in Hou at para 16: :. the proportionality test focuses attention on the scope and complexity of procedure set against the issues and economics of an action and the resources needed to resolve an action, on the identification of the right tool for the particular judicial task. C. Affidavits Expressly Not Required for Streamlined Trial Application [12] As Renke J said in Hou at para 19, necessity is established on the “limited and predicative” materials listed in Rule 8.27(1), which does not mention the use of affidavits to support a streamlined trial application. NPP #2023-02, which provides guidance to both bar and judiciary about how to interpret and apply the streamlined trial rules, states: The Rules do not require that litigants file Affidavits about why the matter is suitable for a Streamlined Trial. That is a matter for argument, based on the Court Record and the submissions of the parties.
